docs.title: 🚀 Jetpack Android Starter
docs.text:
A starting template for modern Android development that takes the pain out of setting up a new project. Built on the foundation of Now In Android's architecture, it provides a starting point for both new and experienced Android developers.

"Android Development is Easy until You Rotate the Device"

docs.title: ☃️ Why This Template?
docs.text:
• Authentication: Firebase authentication with Google Sign-In and email/password
  • Clean Architecture: Clear separation of concerns with a modular, scalable architecture
  • Modern Tech Stack: Latest Android development tools including Jetpack Compose
  • Type-Safe Navigation: Fully typed navigation using Kotlin serialization
  • Robust Data Management: Repository pattern with Room and DataStore
  • Firebase Integration: Auth, Firestore, Analytics, and Crashlytics
  • Background Sync: Data synchronization using WorkManager
  • Multilingual Support: Runtime localization update with support for RTL languages
  • CI/CD: Automated build, release, and deployment with GitHub Actions

Before preparing an app for release, review the sync limitations, state and error-handling limitations, and release checklist. Existing projects also need an upgrade compatibility plan.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The app has two layers: feature modules own screens and ViewModels, and :data owns repository interfaces, implementations, and the models they expose. Data sources in core and Firebase modules handle storage and external services. There is no separate domain module.

Start with the responsibility you need to change:

Change Main home Screen layout, user interactions, screen state feature/* Composables, ViewModels, and screen-data classes Reusable UI, state helpers, navigation infrastructure core/ui, core/navigation Data operations and coordination between sources data repositories Local SQL storage, preferences, REST, authentication, Firestore core/room, core/preferences, core/network, firebase/auth, firebase/firestore Background execution and sync scheduling sync Application assembly, theme, feature entry registration app

Test helpers, lint checks, and profile generation have different roles from application code; including them as ordinary runtime arrows would obscure those boundaries. External libraries and the included build-logic build are omitted; see Build & Tooling for convention plugins and their shared configuration.

docs.title: UI and State Management
docs.text:
A destination's Screen obtains its ViewModel through Hilt and collects state with collectAsStateWithLifecycle(). Screen callbacks invoke ViewModel methods. The ViewModel calls repositories and updates a UiState<T> containing screen data, a loading flag, and a one-time error event. StatefulComposable renders that wrapper.

These are shortened excerpts from HomeViewModel; imports, annotations, and other members are omitted. The actual screen-data property is jetpacks:

data class HomeScreenData(
    val jetpacks: List<Jetpack> = emptyList(),
)

private val _homeUiState = MutableStateFlow(UiState(HomeScreenData()))

val homeUiState = _homeUiState
    .onStart { getJetpacks() }
    .stateInDelayed(UiState(HomeScreenData()), viewModelScope)

fun deleteJetpack(jetpack: Jetpack) {
    _homeUiState.updateWith {
        homeRepository.markJetpackAsDeleted(jetpack)
    }
}

getJetpacks() collects the repository Flow into screen state. Its collector is launched in viewModelScope; lifecycle-aware screen collection does not itself stop that repository collector. Restarting the shared state upstream can launch another collector. See State Management for the helpers and the behavior review in the repair record for the known collector and error-delivery limitations.

docs.title: Data and Dependency Injection
docs.text:
Repositories provide the interface used by ViewModels. Observable reads return Flow, while one-time operations such as saving return Result. Data sources perform the underlying IO.

The source of observed data depends on the repository:

  • Home reads Jetpack rows from Room. Firestore updates reach the screen through writes to Room.
  • Settings and Profile read user preferences from DataStore.
  • Authentication operations call AuthDataSource. After a successful sign-in or registration, AuthRepositoryImpl stores the returned user profile through UserPreferencesDataSource. Home then uses the stored user ID for its list and sync operations. This is an explicit write after an auth operation, not an authentication-listener pipeline.
  • core:network provides Retrofit REST access. An adopter can use REST, Firestore, or coordinate both in a repository according to the feature's needs; Home's sync path currently uses Firestore.

Hilt constructs ViewModels, repositories, and data sources. Repository modules bind implementations to interfaces; data-source modules bind implementations or construct dependencies with @Provides. See Data Layer for construction, dispatchers, and persistence details.

docs.title: The SyncManager Boundary
docs.text:
SyncManager is declared in :data. HomeRepositoryImpl calls that interface to request work. :sync depends on :data and supplies SyncManagerImpl; its SyncModule binds the implementation with @Binds in SingletonComponent. The app includes :sync, allowing Hilt to assemble the graph.

At runtime, a repository can therefore call into the sync implementation without a Gradle data → sync dependency. The worker calls back into HomeRepository.sync(). These runtime calls do not create a module dependency cycle.

docs.title: How It Fits Together
docs.text:
This sequence follows Home's existing operations. The worker portion illustrates a pass scheduled after a local edit; WorkManager controls when it actually starts.

sequenceDiagram
    participant UI as Home / Item screens
    participant VM as Home / Item ViewModels
    participant Repo as HomeRepositoryImpl
    participant Local as Room via LocalDataSource
    participant Manager as SyncManagerImpl / WorkManager
    participant Worker as SyncWorker
    participant Remote as FirebaseDataSource
    UI->>VM: Collect homeUiState with lifecycle
    VM->>Repo: getJetpacks()
    Repo->>Manager: requestSync()
    Note over Repo,Manager: Request happens when getJetpacks() is invoked
    Repo->>Local: Collect getJetpacks(userId)
    Local-->>Repo: Stored rows
    Repo-->>VM: Flow of Jetpack lists
    VM-->>UI: UiState with HomeScreenData
    Note over UI,Local: Item save or Home delete
    UI->>VM: Save / delete callback
    VM->>Repo: createOrUpdateJetpack() / markJetpackAsDeleted()
    Repo->>Local: Store pending change
    Repo->>Manager: requestSync()
    Note over Manager,Worker: Unique one-time work, KEEP policy, connected network constraint
    Manager->>Worker: Run when scheduled
    Worker->>Repo: Collect sync() progress Flow
    Repo->>Local: Snapshot pending rows for user
    loop Pending rows
        Repo->>Remote: Create/update or delete
        Repo->>Local: markAsSynced(id)
    end
    Repo->>Remote: pullJetpacks(userId, cursor)
    Remote-->>Repo: Remote rows
    Repo->>Local: Upsert pulled rows
    Local-->>Repo: Observed row changes
    Repo-->>VM: Updated Jetpack list
    VM-->>UI: Updated screen state

Home starts with its initial empty screen data, then displays Room emissions; it does not wait for a remote response to display stored rows. Sync is request-triggered one-time work, with no periodic schedule configured. getJetpacks() requests work even if its returned Flow is never collected. Save/delete operations request work after recording the local change.

A request made while matching unfinished work exists is ignored by KEEP; that request does not guarantee a later pass. Sync snapshots pending rows once, and push-before-pull does not protect edits made during the pass: acknowledgement can clear a newer edit's pending status, and a pull can overwrite local content. The diagram describes operation order, not a conflict-resolution guarantee. The behavior ledger records these limitations and follow-ups. See Data Layer for the detailed sync path.

docs.title: Domain Layer
docs.text: ViewModels currently call repositories directly. Add a use-case boundary when complex business rules need independent testing or several ViewModels need the same orchestration. A model mapping or a second screen alone does not require a new layer. Keep simple source coordination in a repository and screen-specific state in its ViewModel.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Android convention plugins configure JUnit, coroutines testing, Turbine, Truth, and Robolectric for Android application/library unit tests. Compose test support comes from the Compose configuration. :core:testing supplies shared fakes and MainDispatcherRule to modules that explicitly declare it as a test dependency; it is not automatically added to every module.

For a concrete repository test, read SettingsRepositoryImplTest. It constructs the repository with fake auth and preferences sources, collects getSettings() with Turbine, changes a preference through the repository, and checks the next Flow emission. Other cases verify writes and failed Result values. Run it with:

./gradlew :data:testDebugUnitTest --tests 'dev.atick.data.repository.settings.SettingsRepositoryImplTest'

Use MainDispatcherRule for ViewModel tests that use Dispatchers.Main; see ItemViewModelTest. These examples demonstrate specific behavior; they do not establish sync concurrency, upgrade, or complete application coverage. Adding Features links to further test support.

docs.title: Convention plugins
docs.text:
Every module applies build configuration through one of seven convention plugins in build-logic/convention/src/main/kotlin/, registered as dev.atick.* Gradle plugin IDs and aliased in gradle/libs.versions.toml (jetpack-application, jetpack-library, etc.):

Plugin class ID Applies to What it configures ApplicationConventionPlugin dev.atick.application app com.android.application, Compose compiler, oss-licenses, kotlinx-serialization, Dependency Guard, APK badging tasks, Kotlin/Compose/lint/test config LibraryConventionPlugin dev.atick.library Non-UI modules (data, sync, core/room, ...) com.android.library, kotlinx-serialization, resource prefixing, Kotlin/lint/test config UiLibraryConventionPlugin dev.atick.ui.library Compose modules (core/ui, feature/*) Everything library does, plus the Compose compiler TestConventionPlugin dev.atick.test benchmarks com.android.test, Gradle Managed Devices, Kotlin config DaggerHiltConventionPlugin dev.atick.dagger.hilt Modules using Hilt DI com.google.dagger.hilt.android, KSP FirebaseConventionPlugin dev.atick.firebase firebase/* google-services, Crashlytics DokkaConventionPlugin dev.atick.dokka Every documented module org.jetbrains.dokka

Shared logic each plugin composes lives alongside them as top-level functions, not plugins themselves: configureKotlinAndroid, configureAndroidCompose, configureAndroidLint, configureAndroidTest, configureResourcePrefix, configureBadgingTasks, configureGradleManagedDevices.

docs.title: Apply or extend the build configuration
docs.text:
A Compose feature module applies the existing UI, Hilt and documentation aliases, as feature/home/build.gradle.kts does:

plugins {
    alias(libs.plugins.jetpack.ui.library)
    alias(libs.plugins.jetpack.dagger.hilt)
    alias(libs.plugins.jetpack.dokka)
}

Use jetpack.library for a non-UI Android library. These aliases resolve to the convention plugins above; module-specific configuration still belongs in the module's android and dependencies blocks. Follow the feature guide for module registration and dependencies.

For an approved new dependency, add its version to [versions] and alias to [libraries] in gradle/libs.versions.toml, then consume the generated accessor:

// Existing aliases in core/network/build.gradle.kts:
dependencies {
    implementation(platform(libs.okhttp.bom))
    implementation(libs.okhttp.core)
}

A BOM supplies versions for its member libraries; do not assign competing member versions. For a new external Gradle plugin, add a [plugins] alias. The catalog owns library and plugin versions used through these aliases; the Spotless init script and GitHub workflows also contain explicit tool versions. Editing prose does not move or update them.

.github/renovate.json extends config:recommended, group:all, :dependencyDashboard, and schedule:daily. When adopting the template, enable the Renovate GitHub App for your repository and review its onboarding/dashboard and grouped updates. No Dependabot configuration is supplied. CI commits the regenerated Dependency Guard baseline to Renovate PRs (see Renovate PRs), and gitIgnoredAuthors lists the bot authors of that commit so Renovate keeps rebasing the branch.

Discuss new dependencies, modules, convention-plugin changes, SDK/compiler upgrades and formatting configuration changes before implementing them. To extend a convention plugin after agreement, edit its class/shared helpers in build-logic/convention/src/main/kotlin/; a new plugin also needs registration in build-logic/convention/build.gradle.kts and a catalog alias. Run the convention checks and affected consumer build afterward. Root-relative paths in shared build logic use isolated.rootProject.projectDirectory to support Isolated Projects.

docs.title: Compose compiler stability config
docs.text:
compose_compiler_config.conf (repo root) lists types the Compose compiler should treat as stable even though it can't prove it — currently just dev.atick.data.model.**, the data layer's immutable models:

// Only add types that really are immutable — an entry here is a promise the compiler trusts
// without checking.
dev.atick.data.model.**

Every Compose module reads this file through AndroidCompose.kt (stabilityConfigurationFiles.add(...)). The configuration lets the compiler treat matching types as stable across module boundaries; it does not verify their immutability.

docs.title: Spotless, via an init script
docs.text:
Spotless is applied by gradle/init.gradle.kts when that init script is passed explicitly. Without it, the normal build does not register Spotless tasks. With it, the script applies the plugin to subprojects and defines these targets relative to each project's directory:

Target Files License header Ruleset kotlin **/*.kt spotless/copyright.kt ktlint 1.6.0, android=true, Compose rules 0.6.3 groovy **/*.gradle spotless/copyright.gradle Header insertion kts **/*.kts spotless/copyright.kts Header insertion xml **/*.xml spotless/copyright.xml Header insertion

Each target excludes files under build/. Markdown is not a target, and the root project's own files are outside the subprojects block. The root spotlessCheck invocation checks main-build subprojects, including intermediate grouping projects; it does not run the included build's checks.

Task discovery works when the init script is present: ./gradlew tasks --all --init-script gradle/init.gradle.kts --no-configuration-cache. The included build also registers Spotless tasks when addressed explicitly, but its check currently fails: header paths resolve to the missing build-logic/spotless/copyright.* templates. A successful root check therefore does not establish formatting coverage for convention-plugin sources. Fixing that init-script limitation is a separate build configuration change.

./gradlew spotlessApply --init-script gradle/init.gradle.kts --no-configuration-cache
./gradlew spotlessCheck --init-script gradle/init.gradle.kts --no-configuration-cache

To personalize copyright headers, edit the holder/year in all four spotless/copyright.* templates, run the apply command, and review the resulting source diff before checking it. The XML template is an XML comment; the Kotlin/Gradle templates are block comments. Preserve those wrappers and the init script's header delimiters. Changing targets or rules needs separate agreement.

docs.title: Custom lint (:lint)
docs.text:
Two checks, implemented as a plain java-library module (not a convention-plugin consumer — lint tooling targets an older JVM) and shipped to every consumer automatically:

Check File Severity Flags DesignSystemDetector lint/.../designsystem/DesignSystemDetector.kt ERROR Raw Material3 composables where core/ui provides a wrapper TestMethodNameDetector lint/.../TestMethodNameDetector.kt WARNING @Test methods named test* (the annotation already says it's a test)

Both are registered in JetpackIssueRegistry and reach every module through lintPublish(projects.lint) in core/ui/build.gradle.kts:78 — a module using the design system gets the checks without wiring anything up itself.

Run the check's own unit tests: ./gradlew :lint:test.

docs.title: APK badging
docs.text:
Badging.kt registers three tasks per application variant, comparing aapt2 dump badging output against a committed golden file so a permission, SDK-version, or manifest change is caught in review instead of at release time:

Task (release variant) Does :app:generateReleaseBadging Dumps badging info from the built APK :app:checkReleaseBadging Diffs it against app/release-badging.txt, fails the build on drift :app:updateReleaseBadging Overwrites app/release-badging.txt with the new output

CI runs checkReleaseBadging on every PR (.github/workflows/ci.yml); update the golden file locally with updateReleaseBadging when a change is intentional.

The badging check builds a release APK and can also schedule Crashlytics mapping upload through the release build. For local validation without that upload task, run ./gradlew :app:checkReleaseBadging -x :app:uploadCrashlyticsMappingFileRelease. Passing this check does not establish that the APK uses a production signing key.

docs.title: Dependency Guard
docs.text:
Fails the build when the release runtime classpath drifts from a committed baseline, so a new transitive dependency has to be reviewed rather than arriving unnoticed:

// Regenerate with: ./gradlew :app:dependencyGuardBaseline
dependencyGuard {
    configuration("releaseRuntimeClasspath")
}

Baseline lives at app/dependencies/releaseRuntimeClasspath.txt. ./gradlew :app:dependencyGuard checks it (also run in CI); ./gradlew :app:dependencyGuardBaseline regenerates it.

docs.title: Renovate PRs
docs.text:
The hosted Renovate app cannot run Gradle, so its version bumps never update the baseline. On a pull request opened by renovate[bot] from this repository, the build job in ci.yml regenerates the baseline when the check fails, commits it to the PR branch as 📌 chore(deps): update Dependency Guard baseline [no-task] [skip ci], and runs the remaining checks against it. This follows Now in Android. Every other run, including your own PRs, fork PRs and repository_dispatch, still fails on drift.

  • The bot commit has no checks of its own, because of [skip ci]. Without it, GitHub starts a run for the bot's push and holds it until someone approves it. Renovate rewrites its branch almost daily, which drops the bot commit, so the approval prompt would return every day. The run that made the commit already tested the regenerated baseline. If 🏗️ Build & Test is a required check, merge these PRs as an admin.
  • That job checks out the PR branch (github.head_ref) on Renovate PRs, because git-auto-commit-action cannot push from the default merge ref. Keep that ref: line.
  • APK badging is not updated automatically. A bump that changes merged-manifest permissions still fails APK badging until someone reviews and updates the golden file.

docs.title: Gradle Managed Devices
docs.text:
GradleManagedDevices.kt registers two virtual devices Gradle can boot and tear down itself, so instrumented tests and baseline-profile generation don't depend on whatever's plugged in:

Device API Image Task prefix Pixel 6 33 aosp pixel6Api33 Pixel 4 30 aosp-atd (smaller, automated-test-device) pixel4Api30

dev.atick.test registers these devices in :benchmarks. Its baseline-profile configuration selects pixel6Api33 and disables connected devices. API 33 is the configured generation environment; this is not a minimum API requirement for apps consuming profiles. See the current profile generation requirements. Install the corresponding SDK emulator/system image and enable hardware virtualization. Gradle can download missing device components; running these tasks boots an emulator.

docs.title: Baseline profiles
docs.text:
:benchmarks (BaselineProfileGenerator.kt, StartupBenchmark.kt) generates and measures the app's baseline profile, wired via alias(libs.plugins.baselineprofile) in app/build.gradle.kts:

// app/build.gradle.kts:161-167
baselineProfile {
    automaticGenerationDuringBuild = false
    dexLayoutOptimization = true
}

Important

automaticGenerationDuringBuild = false means the profile is not regenerated automatically — every build would otherwise wait for an emulator. Run ./gradlew :app:generateReleaseBaselineProfile by hand whenever the app's startup path changes.

Generate the startup profile, then measure the two compilation modes in StartupBenchmark:

./gradlew :app:generateReleaseBaselineProfile
./gradlew :benchmarks:pixel6Api33BenchmarkReleaseAndroidTest -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=dev.atick.benchmarks.StartupBenchmark

The class filter keeps the measurement run separate from BaselineProfileGenerator. Generation writes profile sources under app/src/release/generated/baselineProfiles/; review those files when regenerating. Managed-device HTML results are under benchmarks/build/reports/androidTests/managedDevice/; benchmark JSON/traces are in the corresponding benchmarks/build/outputs/managed_device_android_test_additional_output/ tree. Compare timeToInitialDisplayMs for startupNoCompilation and startupWithBaselineProfile; the latter requires a packaged profile. Emulator results help check the harness; use a physical device for representative performance measurements. This generator covers app startup only.

docs.title: Compose compiler metrics and reports
docs.text:
Compile a UI module with both opt-in properties:

./gradlew :feature:home:compileReleaseKotlin -PenableComposeCompilerMetrics=true -PenableComposeCompilerReports=true

AndroidCompose.kt enables each destination only when its property is true. Outputs are relative to the root build directory, retaining the module path: this command writes to build/feature/home/compose-metrics/ and build/feature/home/compose-reports/, not feature/home/build/. Other UI modules use the same layout. If an up-to-date compile has no output, repeat the focused command with --rerun-tasks.

Read the metrics JSON for aggregate counts, the composables text/CSV reports for inferred stability and restartable/skippable functions, and the classes report for unstable fields. Compare reports from the same variant before and after a change. These are compiler decisions, not runtime timings; use Android Studio's Layout Inspector for recomposition inspection and CPU/System Trace profiling for measured work. To inspect app size, build a release APK and open it in Studio's APK Analyzer. Release shrinking is already enabled; investigate release-only failures with Logcat and app/build/outputs/mapping/release/mapping.txt before changing keep rules.

docs.title: Local build configuration
docs.text: The REST client reads BuildConfig.BACKEND_URL. Supply BACKEND_URL=https://your-backend.example/ in root local.properties when adopting a backend, with a trailing slash as Retrofit requires. The secrets plugin uses secrets.defaults.properties as its fallback file; see Firebase setup for the separate GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID input. These values become build configuration, so do not use them to embed server credentials in the app.

docs.title: Gradle build performance
docs.text:
Set in gradle.properties: org.gradle.parallel=true, org.gradle.caching=true, org.gradle.configuration-cache=true (with .parallel=true), and org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx8g -XX:+UseParallelGC -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=2g.

Develocity build scans (settings.gradle.kts:47-56) publish only when a CI environment variable is set, so automatic publication is disabled when CI is absent or empty. A nonempty value such as CI=false still satisfies that predicate; an explicit --scan request is a separate choice.

docs.title: Prepare the application and signing
docs.text:
1. Set the adopted application's ID in app/build.gradle.kts and match it in Firebase, Play Console and fastlane/Appfile. The supplied Appfile still names dev.atick.compose.
  2. Update majorUpdateVersion, minorUpdateVersion, and patchVersion in the app build file. The current formula is major * 10000 + minor * 100 + patch; verify that the resulting versionCode exceeds every version already uploaded to Play. A Git tag does not set the version.
  3. Follow release signing setup. Keep the established signing/upload key for updates. For the workflow's app/key.jks, set storeFile=key.jks in the root signing properties: the build resolves this path relative to app, not the repository root.
  4. Build and test the signed release locally, review CHANGELOG.md, and run the checks listed in Contributing. Keep signing material and service-account keys out of commits.

Caution

Without keystore.properties, the release build falls back to the debug key. Build success alone does not establish that an APK or AAB is correctly signed for publication.

docs.title: Play access and Bundler
docs.text:
Use a managed Ruby environment with Bundler; the release workflow currently selects Ruby 4.0.6, while Gemfile.lock records Bundler 2.7.2 and Fastlane 2.237.0. From the repository root:

bundle install

Use bundle exec for later Fastlane commands so they use the lockfile. Do not run fastlane init over this repository's existing Appfile/Fastfile. See Fastlane installation for Ruby/Bundler setup.

For Play access, create the app in Play Console and complete an initial manual build upload before using Supply. Enable the Google Play Developer API in a Cloud project, create a service account, and invite its email in Play Console's Users and permissions with access to the intended app and release track. Google no longer requires linking the developer account to a Cloud project; follow Google's API setup for current account steps. This workflow uses a downloaded service-account JSON key at fastlane/play-store.json; Firebase's google-services.json is a different file.

The Appfile uses this shape; replace its supplied dev.atick.compose package with your adopted ID. Run Fastlane from the repository root so the key path resolves correctly:

json_key_file("fastlane/play-store.json")
package_name("your.application.id")

After supplying your key and matching package name, these commands validate access and fetch the existing listing; they do not publish a release:

bundle exec fastlane run validate_play_store_json_key json_key:fastlane/play-store.json
bundle exec fastlane supply init

Supply downloads metadata into fastlane/metadata/android/<locale>/. Review titles/descriptions there and add images/screenshots explicitly; the initial download does not retrieve existing screenshots or videos. See Supply setup and metadata.

docs.title: Repository secrets
docs.text:
In the adopted GitHub repository's Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions, add these repository secrets. The table follows .github/workflows/cd.yml; use your own files and values.

Secret Stored format Workflow destination GOOGLE_SERVICES Base64 of Android Firebase configuration JSON app/google-services.json KEYSTORE Base64 of the binary signing keystore app/key.jks KEYSTORE_PROPERTIES Base64 of signing properties (storeFile=key.jks, storePassword, keyAlias, keyPassword) Root keystore.properties GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID Plain web OAuth client ID GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID=… in root local.properties PLAY_STORE_JSON Base64 of the Play service-account JSON key fastlane/play-store.json in the Play job

To encode a file on macOS or Linux without wrapped lines, use the following pattern locally with your own input/output paths, then paste the output into the matching secret:

base64 < /path/to/input-file | tr -d '\r\n' > /path/to/encoded-file

Repeat for the four encoded inputs; paste the web client ID directly. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption: treat encoded copies like the originals. The workflow decodes those four inputs and writes the client ID as text. Both build jobs reconstruct their own signing/Firebase inputs; the Play job additionally reconstructs the service-account key.

docs.title: Lanes, metadata, and publication
docs.text:
Lane Current behavior test Runs Gradle test beta Legacy lane calling assembleRelease then crashlytics; not a working distribution setup for the locked Fastlane version deploy Builds an AAB with bundleRelease, generates English release notes from five commits, then calls upload_to_play_store(validate_only: false)

The legacy Crashlytics Beta action is not present in Fastlane 2.237.0. Firebase Crashlytics crash reporting handles crash reports; a future distribution workflow would need separate configuration, such as Firebase App Distribution. Do not use the supplied beta lane as release instructions.

deploy overwrites fastlane/metadata/android/en-US/changelogs/default.txt. Hand-editing that file before running the lane will lose the edits. Supply prefers <versionCode>.txt over default.txt for that version; other locale notes and listing assets also need review. Changelog files are currently gitignored, so local notes will not reach a tag checkout unless you deliberately change how they are supplied. The release checkout also uses the default shallow history: the lane's five-commit request does not guarantee five commits are available there.

Warning

The supplied deploy lane performs a real upload. With no track/status override, the locked Supply defaults are production and completed. Metadata and images are uploaded too when supplied. Choose and configure your release policy before triggering this workflow; the lane is not a validation-only or internal-testing lane.

Once the adopted repository is configured and the release is reviewed, create a version tag such as v1.3.1 on that revision and push that tag to trigger cd.yml. Tag publication is an explicit release action. The workflow then:

  1. Runs formatting validation and builds a signed APK.
  2. Starts two separate jobs after the APK build: github-release attaches that APK and uses the whole root CHANGELOG.md as the release body; play-store-release rebuilds an AAB with Fastlane and uploads it to Play. Neither publication job waits for the other to succeed.

For a deliberate local Play publication with the same configured lane, the command is bundle exec fastlane android deploy. Generated fastlane/README.md lists lane commands; this section supplies the setup and consequences.

If a release fails, inspect the failed job first. Base64/JSON errors point to secret format; signing errors to the decoded properties, app-relative key path or alias; Play permission errors to API enablement and app access; duplicate-version errors to versionCode. Check listing/draft-app requirements in Play Console for metadata rejection. The APK build has a 45-minute timeout; a successful GitHub release does not establish that Play publication succeeded.

docs.title: Local documentation preview
docs.text:
Run from the repository root after completing Android/JDK setup. Python 3.14 matches docs.yml. The packages below mirror CI; only the admonitions plugin is pinned.

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install mkdocs mkdocs-material mkdocs-github-admonitions-plugin==0.1.1 Pygments
./gradlew dokkaGeneratePublicationHtml -PdocsRevision="$(git rev-parse HEAD)"
.venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p 'test_*.py'
.venv/bin/python scripts/prepare_docs.py
.venv/bin/python -m mkdocs build --strict --config-file build/docs-mkdocs.yml
.venv/bin/python scripts/check_docs.py --site site
.venv/bin/python -m mkdocs serve --config-file build/docs-mkdocs.yml

Open the server URL printed in the terminal (normally http://127.0.0.1:8000/) and stop it with Ctrl+C. Home is available at /, Dokka at /api/, and the benchmark and custom-lint references under Tooling. Run preparation and the strict build again after changing documentation; serve watches the assembled copy rather than the authored guides.

prepare_docs.py requires real build/dokka/html/index.html; it does not create placeholder API pages. It replaces only build/docs-source/, copies authored guides and actual API output there, and generates the README homepage and tooling references. The generated configuration is build/docs-mkdocs.yml. Obsolete API files cannot survive a fresh preparation.

The homepage transformation adjusts Markdown link destinations, preserving external URLs and fragments. Repository-only links and generated source links point to the documented commit. Preparation defaults to HEAD; --revision <full-commit-sha> and Gradle's matching -PdocsRevision=<full-commit-sha> select a different revision. Uncommitted content can be previewed, but remote source links describe the selected commit, not local edits. Historical evidence pins remain unchanged. Module READMEs use absolute main URLs because Dokka treats relative Markdown destinations in those introductions as unresolved references. Preparation rewrites active main links to the selected commit in the assembled site. Use that preview for unmerged documentation; repository README links follow the released guides until merge.

Dokka publishes seventeen application/support modules, including navigation and testing. Each module includes its README introduction. API pages show declared members; superclass links lead to inherited SDK API references. Benchmark and lint READMEs are guide references rather than extra API modules, so documenting them does not change their build configuration. Dokka warnings fail generation. MkDocs validates authored page links and anchors; check_docs.py also checks root/module references and assembled HTML destinations, images, assets and fragments. External URL availability and visual usability still require review.

The thirteen retired guide paths have compatibility pages. Old heading anchors land on those pages, which link to maintained replacements; they do not restore obsolete instructions. The historical homepage URL remains /. Compatibility pages outside navigation remain published.

Pull requests and every push to main, including workflow-only changes, run the same preparation, strict build and link checks. CI validates the PR head commit; it uploads the site as an artifact. A separate deployment job runs only after successful main-push validation and publishes that artifact without rebuilding. Pull-request validation has read-only repository permissions. Local preview commands do not deploy anything.

build/, site/ and .venv/ are ignored. The older generated paths docs/index.md and docs/api/ also remain ignored but are not inputs to the new preparation process. Authored compatibility pages in docs/*.md remain tracked. Do not commit generated output or local environments.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
The shared components in :core:ui provide consistent buttons, inputs, navigation, feedback, and themed backgrounds. Start with the catalog below, use slots and callbacks to supply content and behavior, and change the shared theme when a visual choice should apply across screens.

For a destination's ViewModel/state wiring, follow the feature guide. This page covers component usage, branding, previews, accessibility, localization, and adding reusable UI.

docs.title: Catalog
docs.text: Components live in core/ui/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/core/ui/components/. The file names below identify their implementations; the Core UI API has signatures and KDoc.

docs.title: Buttons — Button.kt
docs.text:
Component Purpose JetpackButton Filled button, high emphasis. Container color is colorScheme.onBackground JetpackOutlinedButton Outlined button, medium emphasis. 1.dp border in colorScheme.outline when enabled JetpackTextButton No background, low emphasis

Each has two overloads: text: @Composable () -> Unit plus an optional leadingIcon, or a bare content: @Composable RowScope.() -> Unit slot for anything else.

Component Purpose DividerWithText HorizontalDivider with centered text (e.g. "OR" between sign-in methods) SwipeToDismiss End-to-start-only SwipeToDismissBox, delete icon + errorContainer background DynamicAsyncImage Coil painter rendered with Image; loading wheel, error/preview placeholder, theme tint AppBackground Theme-driven Surface, resets LocalAbsoluteTonalElevation for nested surfaces AppGradientBackground Dual-gradient Surface, angled 11.06°, colors from LocalGradientColors

Selection state belongs to the caller: pass selected/checked and update it through the callback. JetpackTag's follow appearance does not persist a preference. Keep related state in the screen's existing state model; use local remembered state for purely local UI selection.

The navigation suite calls NavigationSuiteScaffoldDefaults.calculateFromAdaptiveInfo; it does not implement a compact/medium/expanded mapping of its own. Do not assume an expanded window selects a drawer. See Navigation for the app's adaptive content and back stacks.

docs.title: Theming
docs.text: JetpackTheme in core/ui/.../theme/Theme.kt supplies MaterialExpressiveTheme, the shared JetpackTypography, and the background, gradient and tint locals.

docs.title: Brand colors and typography
docs.text:
1. Edit the named color tokens in theme/Color.kt and their roles in both LightDefaultColorScheme and DarkDefaultColorScheme in theme/Theme.kt.
  2. Check paired roles together (primary/onPrimary, surface/onSurface, and container/on-container pairs). A new primary color alone will not recolor every wrapper: JetpackButton, for example, uses onBackground as its container. It has no public colors parameter.
  3. Edit JetpackTypography in theme/Type.kt for shared text roles. It is internal to :core:ui; feature code reads MaterialTheme.typography, rather than importing that declaration.
  4. Preview both themes, disabled states, text over images, and the actual button foreground/background combinations. Check contrast after changing either role; choosing theme tokens does not establish accessibility by itself.

For example, these illustrative arguments replace the matching roles inside a lightColorScheme call in Theme.kt (import androidx.compose.ui.graphics.Color); choose and check a corresponding pair for darkColorScheme too:

primary = Color(0xFF315DA8),
onPrimary = Color.White,

For a local text treatment, use a role or copy it at the point of use. This excerpt belongs inside an existing composable (imports: Material 3 Text/MaterialTheme, androidx.compose.ui.unit.sp):

Text(
    text = title,
    style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleLarge.copy(letterSpacing = 0.sp),
    color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.onSurface,
)

docs.title: Dynamic color
docs.text:
On Android 12+, dynamic color takes precedence unless disableDynamicTheming is true. On older versions the two default schemes are used. To inspect your brand colors consistently, wrap a preview or local component in JetpackTheme(disableDynamicTheming = true).

The running app maps the settings preference useDynamicColor to the theme's inverse disableDynamicTheming argument. Use the existing settings UI to check both choices; changing only the static palette will not change a device using wallpaper colors.

docs.title: Backgrounds, gradients and image tint
docs.text:
AppBackground reads LocalBackgroundTheme. AppGradientBackground accepts gradientColors, whose default comes from LocalGradientColors. A local override can use LocalGradientColors.current.copy(top = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primaryContainer); pass that value to AppGradientBackground(gradientColors = colors) { /* content */ } inside JetpackTheme. These are GradientColors values supplied by LocalGradientColors.

Dynamic color supplies an empty gradient over an elevated surface and a primary-colored LocalTintTheme. The static theme supplies a gradient and no icon tint. To show an untinted photo through DynamicAsyncImage, place it inside CompositionLocalProvider(LocalTintTheme provides TintTheme()) { /* image */ } (runtime CompositionLocalProvider and theme LocalTintTheme/TintTheme imports).

docs.title: Images and loading feedback
docs.text:
DynamicAsyncImage(imageUrl, contentDescription, modifier, placeholder) uses rememberAsyncImagePainter with ContentScale.Crop. It renders a loading wheel during loading and uses its placeholder on error or in inspection mode. It applies the current tint to the whole image, so check photos as well as icons. A null description becomes the string "null" for its loading wheel in the current implementation; inspect that announcement before using the wrapper for decorative images. There is no retry callback or request-builder parameter on this wrapper.

The app's ImageLoaderFactory returns the injected Coil loader from core/network/.../CoilModule.kt. That loader adds SVG support, uses the shared HTTP call factory, and sets respectCacheHeaders(false). Neither the wrapper nor that module enables crossfade. Do not infer freshness or offline guarantees from the loader's existence. Request-specific sizing, transformations or retry UI require an explicit extension or a suitable Coil API; keep such additions separate from theme configuration.

StatefulComposable renders ContainedLoadingIndicator; the two loading-wheel components are alternatives for custom layouts. JetpackOverlayLoadingWheel draws a surface around a loader; it does not establish a modal interaction barrier. Disable or guard actions explicitly when an operation must prevent resubmission. See state contracts for dropped updates while loading, errors, and snackbar event delivery.

SwipeToDismiss supports end-to-start dismissal. Its effect invokes the latest onDelete callback when the remembered state enters the dismissed value; ordinary recomposition does not repeat the call. This is not a durable exactly-once guarantee. Keep list identity stable, remove deleted rows through the observed data, and provide an accessible alternative delete action when extending the screen. The existing home flow has no undo action.

docs.title: Previews
docs.text:
Use the shared annotations from dev.atick.core.ui.utils with a parameterless composable that supplies sample data and callbacks. Preview a presentational child rather than a destination that requires an injected ViewModel. This does not require adding Route wrappers to the screen pattern.

@PreviewDevices defines phone, landscape, foldable and tablet configurations. @PreviewThemes defines light and dark configurations. Applying both adds their independent previews; it does not create eight device/theme combinations. For a particular combination, declare an explicit @Preview(device = "spec:width=1280dp,height=800dp,dpi=480", uiMode = Configuration.UI_MODE_NIGHT_YES). See Android's multipreview documentation.

The extension example below includes a complete preview. Add explicit previews with locale = "ar" and fontScale = 1.5f for language and larger-text checks. Wrap in JetpackTheme, use deterministic sample data, and avoid network/database work. When rendering fails, inspect the preview exception, module build, resource availability, and any ViewModel or unavailable platform dependency. Compose formatting rules are separate from rendering failures; follow nearby previews and the formatting workflow. Previews help inspect layout; exercise interactions and assistive technology in a running app too.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
• Give icon-only actions a localized action description. Use contentDescription = null for an icon whose adjacent text already conveys the same meaning, or for a decorative image.
  • Keep touch targets at least 48.dp and check the focus order. Do not shrink targets to match small artwork. Give grouped custom choices selection semantics and an appropriate role; a visual background change alone does not expose selection to accessibility services.
  • Check TalkBack output for names, roles, selected/disabled state, and validation messages. Use Compose error semantics for errors and an appropriate liveRegion for changing status text when needed; avoid repeated announcements on every recomposition. These are extension guidance, not guarantees that every current wrapper announces every state.
  • Check loading feedback while content remains visible, and check focus after an error or deletion. Ensure important actions can be reached without a swipe gesture.
  • Check light/dark and dynamic/static contrast, large system fonts, long translations, and RTL. Avoid fixed-height text containers that clip enlarged labels. Use Accessibility Scanner and manual TalkBack checks on a device/emulator; a successful preview does not prove accessibility.

docs.title: Localization
docs.text:
The current picker offers English and Arabic. To add another language, update the whole path:

  1. Add translated values-<language>/strings.xml files beside the relevant modules' default strings. Keep library prefixes, such as feature_settings_* or core_ui_*; retain default values for fallback and preserve formatting placeholders. Use stringResource for UI labels.
  2. Add a code to Language in data/.../model/settings/Settings.kt, for example FRENCH("fr").
  3. Add the new branch in getLanguageOptions() in SettingsDialog.kt, with a prefixed string resource for the language name and an icon. Options follow Language.entries, so keep their ordering consistent with the selected-index mapping.
  4. Extend SettingsViewModel.getPreferredLanguage() to map "fr" to the new entry. Currently only "ar" is recognized explicitly; all other locales map to English. Adding resources alone would leave the picker showing English for the new locale.
  5. Keep updateLanguagePreference calling setLanguagePreference(language.code). That delegates to AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales; getPreferredLocale() reads application locales and falls back to the system locale. Settings overlays this language onto repository settings; it is not a DataStore language field.
  6. Check the app's generateLocaleConfig = true and res/resources.properties (unqualifiedResLocale=en-US). Locale configuration is generated from resources; do not add a competing handwritten config. The manifest enables RTL and AppCompat's autoStoreLocales metadata. Preserve that wiring when adopting the template.
  7. Build, choose the language in the app and system app-language settings where available, restart, and check picker selection and persistence. Inspect Arabic/RTL layout, directional icons, start/end padding, long labels and formatted values. Preview locale alone does not test storage or activity recreation. Test on pre-33 and 33+ Android when changing locale integration.

docs.title: UiText and form errors
docs.text:
UiText in dev.atick.core.ui.utils carries either DynamicString(value) or StringResource(resId, vararg args). Resolve it at the UI boundary with composable asString(), or asString(context) outside composition. For example, an adopter can add <string name="feature_home_item_count">%1$d items</string> to the home module and render Text(UiText.StringResource(R.string.feature_home_item_count, count).asString()). R must be that module's resource class. Use plurals for proper quantity-sensitive translations; this string example demonstrates formatting arguments only.

TextFieldData.errorMessage is currently String?, not UiText?. An auth form passes its value/errorMessage to JetpackTextField and sends changes back to the ViewModel. The nullable string extensions in dev.atick.core.extensions are isEmailValid(), isPasswordValid(), and isValidFullName(). This excerpt belongs in an auth state update, with invalidEmailMessage a caller-supplied localized string:

copy(
    email = TextFieldData(
        value = email,
        errorMessage = if (email.isEmailValid()) null else invalidEmailMessage,
    ),
)

Use the existing sign-in/sign-up screen and ViewModel for the complete flow; their current validation messages are hardcoded English strings. Localize those messages separately when adopting the form. Password validation requires 8–20 characters, at least one lowercase letter and digit. The full-name check splits on spaces and tests letters; it is a template policy, not a universal definition of a valid name. Revisit these rules for your audience and backend. A null error only means no error is stored; it does not prove that validation ran or the backend will accept the input.

docs.title: Permission helpers
docs.text:
The Activity extensions are in dev.atick.core.ui.extensions; getActivity() is a separate Context extension in dev.atick.core.extensions (:core:android). Register permissionLauncher(onSuccess, onFailure) during Activity initialization, before the Activity is started. Launch it in response to the relevant user action rather than registering a launcher from a click callback or recomposition.

The following complete illustrative Activity adds no manifest permission. It demonstrates the existing helper using POST_NOTIFICATIONS, which the app already declares; keep the existing MainActivity as your app entry point. Imports are shown because launcher timing matters here.

import android.Manifest
import android.os.Build
import android.os.Bundle
import androidx.activity.ComponentActivity
import androidx.activity.result.ActivityResultLauncher
import dev.atick.core.ui.extensions.permissionLauncher

class NotificationPermissionExampleActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    private lateinit var notifications: ActivityResultLauncher<Array<String>>

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        notifications = permissionLauncher(
            onSuccess = { onNotificationsAvailable() },
            onFailure = { onNotificationsDeclined() },
        )
    }

    // Call from your notification opt-in UI after the Activity has been created.
    fun requestNotifications() {
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.TIRAMISU) {
            notifications.launch(arrayOf(Manifest.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS))
        } else {
            onNotificationsAvailable()
        }
    }

    private fun onNotificationsAvailable() { /* Continue your notification flow. */ }
    private fun onNotificationsDeclined() { /* Explain the unavailable feature in your UI. */ }
}

The higher-level checkForPermissions(permissions, onSuccess) requests missing permissions and opens app settings on denial. If all permissions are already granted, it returns without calling onSuccess. It also registers its launcher internally, so it is not a general-purpose helper to call from arbitrary later click handlers. Prefer the registered launcher pattern above for a user-driven flow. Keep denial, already-granted, unsupported-API, and returning-from-settings paths explicit; do not rely on a success callback after returning from system settings.

docs.title: Add a shared component
docs.text:
Keep feature-specific UI next to its screen. Move UI into :core:ui when multiple features need the same contract. Compose existing wrappers first; when adding a new Material wrapper, follow neighboring component APIs and the enforcement rules.

This complete illustrative addition belongs in core/ui/.../components/RetryButton.kt; it is not an existing API. The caller owns loading state and the retry operation. label lets the caller supply localized text, so this example adds no resource. If it supplied its own strings, their names would need the core_ui_ prefix.

import androidx.compose.material3.Text
import androidx.compose.runtime.Composable
import androidx.compose.ui.Modifier
import dev.atick.core.ui.components.JetpackOutlinedButton
import dev.atick.core.ui.theme.JetpackTheme
import dev.atick.core.ui.utils.PreviewThemes

/** Requests another attempt using caller-owned state and behavior. */
@Composable
fun RetryButton(
    label: String,
    onRetry: () -> Unit,
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier,
    enabled: Boolean = true,
) {
    JetpackOutlinedButton(
        onClick = onRetry,
        text = { Text(label) },
        modifier = modifier,
        enabled = enabled,
    )
}

@PreviewThemes
@Composable
private fun RetryButtonPreview() {
    JetpackTheme(disableDynamicTheming = true) {
        RetryButton(label = "Try again", onRetry = {})
    }
}

Use package dev.atick.core.ui.components when adding this file; imports are shown for a standalone example. Keep shared components small and named by behavior. Add meaningful interaction/semantics coverage when introducing behavior: callback on click, disabled state, and accessible label are useful checks for an interactive extension. The existing SwipeToDismissTest demonstrates Compose interaction testing in this module.

For local tabs, hoist the selected index; the caller renders the corresponding content. This excerpt belongs in an existing composable with nonempty titles, selectedIndex in range, and an onSelect: (Int) -> Unit callback (imports: core UI JetpackTabRow/JetpackTab, Material 3 Text):

JetpackTabRow(selectedTabIndex = selectedIndex) {
    titles.forEachIndexed { index, title ->
        JetpackTab(
            selected = selectedIndex == index,
            onClick = { onSelect(index) },
            text = { Text(title) },
        )
    }
}

docs.title: Performance checks
docs.text:
Profile before changing composition structure; use the compiler reports and profiling workflow. In lists, use stable item keys as HomeScreen does, so remembered state stays with its item when rows move. For mixed row layouts, consider contentType for reuse; that is extension guidance, not a claim that the current homogeneous list needs it. Move costly sorting/formatting out of repeated item composition and measure the result. Avoid blanket rules to wrap every callback or use derivedStateOf for every value.

@Immutable and stability configuration declare contracts to Compose; they do not freeze mutable objects. Keep screen data consistent with those contracts and inspect compiler reports when investigating skips/recomposition. For images, inspect request sizes, cropping, scrolling and loading/error states with the actual loader. Test on a device with realistic content; a preview is not a rendering-performance benchmark.

docs.title: Enforcement
docs.text:
DesignSystemDetector (lint/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/lint/designsystem/DesignSystemDetector.kt) is an ERROR-severity lint check, published to every module that depends on core/ui via lintPublish(projects.lint) (core/ui/build.gradle.kts) — no per-module wiring needed.

It flags a call by where it resolves, not by name (UCallExpression.resolvePackageName()), so a same-named Tab or Icon from another library isn't misflagged. Only calls resolving to androidx.compose.material3 and matching an entry in DesignSystemDetector.METHOD_NAMES trigger it — Button → JetpackButton, TextField/OutlinedTextField → JetpackTextField, all five *TopAppBar variants → JetpackTopAppBar, FilterChip/ElevatedFilterChip → JetpackFilterChip, NavigationBar(Item)/NavigationRail(Item) → their Jetpack* equivalents, TabRow/Tab → JetpackTabRow/JetpackTab, the four icon-toggle-button variants → JetpackIconToggleButton, and ExtendedFloatingActionButton → JetpackExtendedFab. Calls inside dev.atick.core.ui.components itself — the wrappers' own definitions — are exempt, since they must call the Material composables they wrap.

When adding a wrapper for a Material API that should be standardized across features, update DesignSystemDetector.METHOD_NAMES and the detector tests in :lint. Cover the mapped Material call, an unrelated same-named API, and the wrappers' package exemption. Run ./gradlew :lint:test. A composite such as the illustrative retry button, built from existing wrappers, does not need a new substitution merely because it is shared. Do not edit the detector just to make an example pass.

docs.title: Data Layer
docs.text: Repositories combine data sources and expose data to ViewModels. This guide explains how to choose storage, wire dependencies, extend persistence, and follow the Home feature's current sync behavior. See Architecture for the module graph.

docs.title: Data sources
docs.text:
Choose the pattern for the feature rather than adding every source to every repository:

Reader need Source and existing example Behavior Small local settings/profile Typed JSON DataStore; SettingsRepositoryImpl, ProfileRepositoryImpl Observe preferences as a Flow; update the serialized object locally. Auth sign-out is a separate operation. Relational local data with background remote access Room and Firestore; HomeRepositoryImpl Screens observe Room; local writes request background sync. See the limitations below. Explicit REST request Retrofit; NetworkDataSource.getPosts() / getPost(id) Suspend calls return DTOs or throw. No supplied repository connects these posts to a screen or persists them. Authentication Firebase Auth; AuthRepositoryImpl Sign in/register through the auth source, then store profile fields in preferences.

For a REST-only extension, add a repository interface and constructor-injected implementation in :data, bind it in RepositoryModule, and map NetworkPost into your feature's data model. Wrap one-time requests in suspendRunCatching. Add observable local storage only if the feature needs it; a successful request alone does not supply an offline cache or a freshness policy.

The existing REST implementation moves the request to its injected dispatcher:

// NetworkDataSourceImpl method excerpt; constructor/imports omitted.
override suspend fun getPosts(): List<NetworkPost> {
    return withContext(ioDispatcher) {
        jetpackRestApi.getPosts()
    }
}

Firestore snapshot listeners, TTL caching, and a manual refresh UI are possible extensions, not current Home behavior. A listener needs its own subscription cleanup and local merge policy; a cache needs an explicit expiry/refresh policy. The existing Firestore pull uses get(), not a listener.

docs.title: Repository pattern
docs.text:
Home exposes observable Room data and one-time local operations:

// HomeRepository interface excerpt; package/imports omitted.
interface HomeRepository : Syncable {
    fun getJetpacks(): Flow<List<Jetpack>>
    fun getJetpack(id: String): Flow<Jetpack>
    suspend fun createOrUpdateJetpack(jetpack: Jetpack): Result<Unit>
    suspend fun markJetpackAsDeleted(jetpack: Jetpack): Result<Unit>
}

HomeRepositoryImpl.getJetpacks() calls requestSync() when the method constructs the Flow, including when nobody collects it. Collection then reads the user ID from preferences and observes that user's non-deleted Room rows. getJetpack(id) observes the DAO by ID and does not request sync.

Creation/update stamps lastUpdated, sets needsSync=true and action UPSERT, writes Room, then requests sync. Deletion flags the existing row deleted=true, needsSync=true, action DELETE, then requests sync. This hides it from the list without immediately removing the local row.

A successful local operation does not acknowledge a remote upload. Authentication lookup, database access, and requesting work can fail. If requesting work throws after Room commits, the repository returns failure even though the local change remains. WorkManager's eventual outcome is not awaited by requestSync(), which returns Unit.

docs.title: Result via suspendRunCatching
docs.text:
One-time repository operations use this helper from core/android:

// CoroutineUtils.kt function excerpt; imports omitted.
suspend inline fun <T> suspendRunCatching(crossinline block: suspend () -> T): Result<T> {
    return try {
        Result.success(block())
    } catch (cancellationException: CancellationException) {
        throw cancellationException
    } catch (exception: Exception) {
        Result.failure(exception)
    }
}

It converts ordinary Exceptions to failed Results and rethrows cancellation. It does not wrap later emissions from a returned Flow. Data-source suspend calls may throw; observation failures must be handled in the collecting pipeline. flowOn(ioDispatcher) moves upstream work but does not catch errors. The state update helpers inspect returned Results; they do not catch arbitrary thrown exceptions or guarantee cleanup on cancellation. See State Management.

REST transport failures can surface as IOException, unsuccessful HTTP responses as Retrofit HttpException, and response decoding failures as serialization exceptions. A repository's failed Result lets the caller choose a response; no generic automatic retry or sign-out policy is supplied for these errors. A 401 response, for example, needs the API's authentication policy rather than an unconditional reset of local user data.

docs.title: Dependency injection
docs.text:
Use constructor injection for implementations whose dependencies are supplied by the graph. RepositoryModule in :data binds their interfaces:

// RepositoryModule class excerpt; other bindings and imports omitted.
@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
abstract class RepositoryModule {
    @Binds
    @Singleton
    internal abstract fun bindHomeRepository(
        homeRepositoryImpl: HomeRepositoryImpl,
    ): HomeRepository
}

@Binds tells Hilt which implementation supplies an interface. Its @Inject constructor describes construction. @Provides supplies types requiring a builder, factory, or other construction logic:

Provider Construction Graph location DatabaseModule.provideRoomDatabase Room.databaseBuilder(...) core/room/di DaoModule.provideJetpackDao jetpackDatabase.getJetpackDao() core/room/di RetrofitModule.provideRetrofitClient Retrofit builder, converter, OkHttp client, BuildConfig.BACKEND_URL core/network/di/retrofit RestApiModule.provideApiService retrofit.create(JetpackRestApi::class.java) core/network/di DatastoreModule.providePreferencesDataStore DataStoreFactory.create(...) core/preferences/di CredentialManagerModule.provideCredentialManager CredentialManager.create(context) firebase/auth/di

For example, these provider excerpts show Room and Retrofit construction. Containing modules, imports, and private constants are omitted; these are existing providers, not additional bindings:

// DatabaseModule
@Singleton
@Provides
fun provideRoomDatabase(@ApplicationContext appContext: Context): JetpackDatabase {
    return Room.databaseBuilder(
        appContext,
        JetpackDatabase::class.java,
        ROOM_DATABASE_NAME,
    ).fallbackToDestructiveMigration(true).build()
}

// RestApiModule
@Singleton
@Provides
fun provideApiService(retrofit: Retrofit): JetpackRestApi {
    return retrofit.create(JetpackRestApi::class.java)
}

The Room fallback is current configuration with data-loss consequences, explained below; do not copy it as a data-preserving upgrade policy. The DataStore provider appears in its storage section.

These providers and the repository bindings use SingletonComponent; @Singleton shares a scoped binding within that component. Installation and scope are separate: installing a module does not scope every binding in it. @Module(includes=[...]) includes bindings, not a processing order. @ViewModelScoped and @ActivityScoped are alternative lifetimes when extending the graph, not the storage/repository scopes shown here. For custom components, entry points, or multibindings, consult the maintained Hilt documentation before extending this setup.

Qualifiers distinguish values with the same Kotlin type. DispatcherModule in core/android/di provides @IoDispatcher for I/O, @DefaultDispatcher for CPU work, and @MainDispatcher for work requiring the main thread. Data sources inject @IoDispatcher and use withContext for suspend work or flowOn for upstream Flow work. Android factories inject @ApplicationContext Context; for example, the DataStore provider below uses the app's private file location.

Android-created entry points use field injection where appropriate: App is @HiltAndroidApp, and MainActivity is @AndroidEntryPoint with injected fields. Keep repository/data-source construction in Hilt. Runtime arguments for keyed ViewModels follow the Navigation assisted-injection walkthrough; workers use the delegation path below.

Unit tests can supply fakes directly to constructors without starting Hilt:

// Setup excerpt from SettingsRepositoryImplTest; test methods/imports omitted.
private val preferences = FakeUserPreferencesDataSource()
private val auth = FakeAuthDataSource()
private val repository = SettingsRepositoryImpl(
    authDataSource = auth,
    userPreferencesDataSource = preferences,
)

That test collects settings through Turbine, checks writes, and checks failed sign-out Results. See Architecture testing for its runnable command and Guide for feature integration. Hilt instrumentation replacement is a separate test setup; constructor-supplied fakes do not require it.

docs.title: Typed JSON DataStore
docs.text:
UserDataPreferences is a Kotlin serialization data class stored in user_preferences.json. It is neither SharedPreferences nor a Protocol Buffers schema. The singleton provider is:

// DatastoreModule provider excerpt; containing module and imports omitted.
@Singleton
@Provides
fun providePreferencesDataStore(
    @ApplicationContext appContext: Context,
    @IoDispatcher ioDispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher,
): DataStore<UserDataPreferences> {
    return DataStoreFactory.create(
        serializer = UserDataSerializer,
        produceFile = { appContext.dataStoreFile(DATA_STORE_FILE_NAME) },
        scope = CoroutineScope(ioDispatcher + SupervisorJob()),
    )
}

DATA_STORE_FILE_NAME is the module's private constant, "user_preferences.json". Reads expose datastore.data.flowOn(ioDispatcher); writes use updateData { old -> old.copy(...) } on the whole object. Keep one DataStore instance per file.

For example, an existing single-setting write preserves the other fields:

// UserPreferencesDataSourceImpl method excerpt; constructor/imports omitted.
override suspend fun setDynamicColorPreference(useDynamicColor: Boolean) {
    withContext(ioDispatcher) {
        datastore.updateData { userData ->
            userData.copy(useDynamicColor = useDynamicColor)
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Defaults, evolution, and reset
docs.text:
• UserDataSerializer.defaultValue is UserDataPreferences(): empty ID, nullable name/picture, follow-system theme, and dynamic color enabled. It supplies a new store's initial value.
  • Missing JSON fields with declared defaults decode to those defaults. The serializer uses the default Json configuration: unknown keys and invalid enum values are not ignored. Renames, removals, and mixed app versions therefore need compatibility review rather than an assumed transparent upgrade.
  • readFrom() translates SerializationException into CorruptionException. No corruption handler is configured in DatastoreModule; malformed/truncated JSON does not automatically reset to defaults. Other I/O failures can also propagate to readers.
  • resetUserPreferences() writes a new default object, including resetting theme/color choices. Profile and Settings sign-out call auth sign-out first, then reset preferences; a failed auth sign-out leaves preferences untouched. Resetting preferences does not clear Room or Firestore.

To add a preference, add a serializable property with an intentional default to UserDataPreferences, add a method to UserPreferencesDataSource and its implementation using updateData, then expose it through the relevant repository model/mapping and operation. Bind the UI to that repository. Test old JSON missing the property, round trips, invalid values, reset behavior, and repository mapping. Preserve existing fields in each copy; do not replace the whole object for a single setting. Check serializer compatibility before changing field names or types.

docs.title: Room persistence and schema changes
docs.text:
For a new stored type, follow the existing Jetpack wiring:

  1. Add a Room @Entity with a primary key and a DAO with the required observations/mutations.
  2. Register the entity in JetpackDatabase.entities and expose its DAO from the database.
  3. Provide the DAO through DaoModule; expose it through a data-source interface/implementation and bind that implementation in DataSourceModule.
  4. Add repository model mappings and operations, including user filtering and pending metadata if the new type participates in sync. Adding a Room entity alone does not add a Firestore protocol.
  5. Increase the database version for schema changes and register a data-preserving migration in DatabaseModule. Test a file-backed upgrade with existing and pending rows, then test DAO behavior. Schema export and migration-test configuration need to be established; the current database has exportSchema=false, and the existing in-memory DAO tests do not validate upgrades.

The current database is version 2. Its provider calls Room.databaseBuilder(appContext, JetpackDatabase::class.java, ROOM_DATABASE_NAME) followed by fallbackToDestructiveMigration(true).build(), with no registered 1 → 2 migration.

Warning

An existing version 1 install can lose its local data, including unsent edits/deletes, when Room recreates tables because no migration path exists. Re-fetching Firestore cannot restore changes that were never uploaded. A same-version schema-integrity failure is a different case; destructive migration is not a general recovery mechanism for editing entities without a version bump.

Plan a preservation strategy before shipping an upgrade; the current configuration does not supply a data-preserving migration. See existing installs and documents for the related Firestore compatibility requirements.

docs.title: Mapping stored and remote models
docs.text:
Keep screen-facing Jetpack values, JetpackEntity, and FirebaseJetpack mappings in :data. For example, the existing pull mapper carries remote metadata and uses entity defaults for local pending flags:

// Jetpack.kt mapping excerpt; package/imports omitted.
fun FirebaseJetpack.toJetpackEntity(): JetpackEntity {
    return JetpackEntity(
        id = id,
        name = name,
        price = price,
        userId = userId,
        lastUpdated = lastUpdated,
        lastSynced = lastSynced,
        serverUpdatedAtNanos = serverUpdatedAtNanos(),
        deleted = deleted,
    )
}

Local create/update separately applies user ID, edit time, and pending metadata in the repository; do not assume the screen model's mapper sets all sync fields. The reverse remote mapper carries content and device timestamps but leaves the server timestamp null for Firestore to assign.

docs.title: Two-way sync
docs.text:
The SyncManager contract lives in :data; :sync binds SyncManagerImpl, which requests unique one-time WorkManager work through Sync.initialize(). There is no periodic sync configured. ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP ignores a request while matching unfinished work exists; it does not queue a second pass behind the active one.

SyncWorker.startUpSyncWork() constructs a DelegatingWorker request carrying the target worker class. The delegating factory path uses Hilt to construct SyncWorker; @Assisted Context and WorkerParameters come from WorkManager, while the repository and dispatcher come from Hilt. The only explicit constraint is NetworkType.CONNECTED. The request is expedited, with RUN_AS_NON_EXPEDITED_WORK_REQUEST when quota is unavailable. Connectivity does not prove Firebase is reachable, and requesting expedited work does not guarantee an immediate start.

docs.title: Algorithm and metadata
docs.text:
Collecting HomeRepositoryImpl.sync() performs these steps:

  1. Read the authenticated user ID from DataStore.
  2. Read one snapshot of rows matching lastUpdated > lastSynced OR needsSync = 1 for that user.
  3. For each row, upload UPSERT, hard-delete the remote document for DELETE, or perform no remote operation for NONE. After that branch succeeds, call markAsSynced(id) and emit push progress. Acknowledgement clears needsSync/action and stamps a local millisecond lastSynced.
  4. Read MAX(serverUpdatedAtNanos) for the user, including soft-deleted rows (use zero if absent).
  5. Query Firestore with strict serverUpdatedAt > cursor, then individually upsert each returned mapped entity into Room and emit pull progress. This is not a single transactional batch.
Field Units/source Used by the current implementation lastUpdated Epoch milliseconds, editing device Set on create/update; list ordering/display and pending query comparison with lastSynced. Carried to/from Firestore. lastSynced Epoch milliseconds, uploading device Set in the uploaded model and separately on local acknowledgement; pending query input. Carried back from Firestore, not local-only. needsSync / syncAction Local boolean/action Explicit pending flag and push operation; pulled mappings use defaults false / NONE. deleted Boolean carried to/from Firestore Local soft-delete marker; list query excludes it. The normal delete push hard-deletes the remote document. serverUpdatedAt / serverUpdatedAtNanos Firestore timestamp / epoch nanoseconds in Room Server write time used for the strict pull cursor. Includes timestamps on locally deleted rows.

JetpackEntity.toFirebaseJetpack() leaves @get:ServerTimestamp serverUpdatedAt null, so Firestore fills it on write. The pull mapping copies that value into serverUpdatedAtNanos, retaining nanosecond precision. A write does not directly store its assigned server timestamp in Room; a later pull can do that. This is not an exactly-once echo guarantee. The example security rules require serverUpdatedAt == request.time; the annotation alone does not enforce what other clients may write.

Soft-deleted rows are retained locally after successful remote deletion. There is no scheduled cleanup. Their stored server timestamps remain part of the cursor. A remote hard delete supplies no document or tombstone to the incremental pull, so it does not remove another device's existing local copy.

sequenceDiagram
    participant W as SyncWorker
    participant R as HomeRepositoryImpl
    participant L as Room (local)
    participant F as Firestore (remote)

    W->>R: collect sync()
    R->>L: getUnsyncedJetpacks(userId), one snapshot
    loop each pending entity
        R->>F: upsert or hard delete (NONE skips remote)
        R->>L: markAsSynced(id)
        R-->>W: push progress
    end
    R->>L: getSyncCursor(userId), includes deleted rows
    R->>F: pullJetpacks(userId, syncedAfterNanos)
    loop each returned entity
        R->>L: upsertJetpack(remoteJetpack)
        R-->>W: pull progress
    end

docs.title: Delivery and conflict limitations
docs.text:
Push-before-pull describes ordering, not conflict protection:

  • A row written after the pending snapshot waits for another pass. A request dropped by KEEP does not guarantee that pass; there is no automatic drain loop.
  • Acknowledgement is by ID, not uploaded version. An edit made during upload can lose its pending status. The subsequent unconditional pull upsert can overwrite newer local content.
  • A failed pull can leave a committed prefix. A strict timestamp-only cursor can skip an unapplied document sharing the last stored timestamp. Retrying later distinct timestamps does not resolve that equal-timestamp boundary.
  • Firestore get() uses the SDK's default source, which can return cached data when the server is unavailable. The mapping discards snapshot metadata, so successful completion does not establish that the result was a complete server snapshot. Cache-gap behavior still needs SDK integration verification.

These limitations are recorded for separate sync-consistency and pull-checkpoint work. Do not infer eventual delivery, conflict resolution, or multi-device deletion propagation from a successful pass. Legacy documents missing serverUpdatedAt are excluded even with cursor zero; legacy writers and new rules also need a staged compatibility plan. Follow the upgrade guidance before updating an existing project.

docs.title: Progress, retries, and errors
docs.text:
SyncWorker collects the repository's cold progress Flow on @IoDispatcher, calls setForeground before collection, and updates notification counts after each emitted item. SyncProgress carries total, current, and a message; totals restart between push and pull. An empty phase emits no item progress. The current notification uses the counts, not the progress message.

For a running indicator, observe SyncManager.isSyncing in a ViewModel and expose it as state for lifecycle-aware UI collection. It is true only for RUNNING work, not work waiting on constraints, retry delay, or completion. It is not an upload acknowledgement or detailed progress API. A manual refresh button would be an extension; the Home UI does not currently provide one.

The worker returns success if collection finishes. Its catch (Exception) requests retry while runAttemptCount < TOTAL_SYNC_ATTEMPTS (3): up to four attempts in total, with retry returned on failure at counts 0, 1, and 2 and failure returned on an exception at count 3. No custom backoff is set; WorkManager's default is exponential starting at 30 seconds (nominally 30, 60, 120 seconds for these retries). Constraints and system scheduling can delay execution further.

The catch also includes CancellationException; it does not explicitly preserve cancellation as suspendRunCatching does. This is a recorded lifecycle follow-up, not a guarantee that cancelled work will retry. Earlier local acknowledgements/upserts are not rolled back when a later operation fails. Inspect WorkManager state and worker logs when diagnosing sync; see Sync troubleshooting.
