docs.title: Firebase Setup
docs.text:
This project separates authentication (firebase:auth), Firestore access (firebase:firestore), and crash reporting (firebase:analytics). The app's Firebase convention plugin also adds Analytics and Performance SDK dependencies. The reporting module's name does not describe all app telemetry; see Crashlytics below.

The template configuration supports building the app. Use your own Firebase project to test services.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Google account and access to the Firebase Console
  • A checkout that builds locally (see Getting Started)
  • A device or emulator with Google Play services for Google Sign-In

docs.title: Firebase Console Setup
docs.text:
1. Create a Firebase project and register an Android app with the checkout's application ID, currently dev.atick.compose in app/build.gradle.kts.

  2. Run ./gradlew signingReport (or the Signing Report IDE configuration). Add the SHA-1 fingerprint for the variant you will test under Project Settings → Your apps → SHA certificate fingerprints. Register the release certificate too when testing a signed release; for Play installs, use the Play App Signing certificate rather than only the upload certificate.

  3. Under Authentication → Sign-in method, enable Google and Email/Password. Complete Google's project support-email settings when prompted.

  4. Create a Cloud Firestore database in production mode. The app uses the default database; publish the rules below before testing sync.

  5. After enabling Google and registering fingerprints, download the updated google-services.json for this Android app from Project Settings.

If you replace the template application ID, register that exact new ID and its signing fingerprints, then download the matching configuration. Changing a Kotlin package or namespace alone does not change the application ID. A separate Firebase project/build variant for each environment requires adopter configuration; the template does not provide those environments.

docs.title: Local Project Setup
docs.text:
1. Replace app/google-services.json with the downloaded file. Its Android client must match the application's ID and Firebase project.

  2. In the same Google Cloud project, open APIs & Services → Credentials and find the OAuth 2.0 client whose application type is Web application. The Google provider's Web SDK configuration in Firebase Authentication also exposes its web client ID. Use that client ID, not the Android OAuth client ID.

  3. Add the following to root local.properties, preserving its existing sdk.dir entry:

    GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID=your-web-client-id.apps.googleusercontent.com

    The Secrets Gradle plugin in firebase/auth/build.gradle.kts reads this ignored file and generates BuildConfig.GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID; Config.WEB_CLIENT_ID supplies it to Credential Manager. secrets.defaults.properties supplies a buildable fallback when a local value is absent. That fallback is not configuration for your Firebase project. Downloading the JSON does not set this separately consumed property. See the official Google authentication setup.

  4. Rebuild and run with ./gradlew installDebug, then launch the app. Follow the verification steps after the rules section.

docs.title: Keeping local configuration out of commits
docs.text:
local.properties is ignored. The template app/google-services.json is already tracked, so the ignore rule for that filename does not prevent changes to it from being committed. Keep your project-specific replacement out of commits to this starter repository.

If you use an index hint to reduce local diff noise, set it before replacing the template:

git update-index --skip-worktree app/google-services.json

This leaves the file tracked. It is neither a security control nor protection against every Git operation. Inspect the flag (an S prefix means skip-worktree) and undo it with:

git ls-files -v -- app/google-services.json
git update-index --no-skip-worktree app/google-services.json

Review configuration changes before staging; do not rely on the hint to hide them permanently.

docs.title: Credential Manager: Sign-In vs. Register
docs.text:
Google auth goes through Android's Credential Manager API (firebase/auth/.../AuthDataSourceImpl.kt), which builds two different requests depending on whether the user is signing in or registering:

private fun getSignInRequest(): GetCredentialRequest {
    val getPasswordOption = GetPasswordOption()
    val getGoogleIdOption = GetGoogleIdOption.Builder().setFilterByAuthorizedAccounts(true)
        .setServerClientId(Config.WEB_CLIENT_ID).setAutoSelectEnabled(false).build()
    return GetCredentialRequest
        .Builder()
        .addCredentialOption(getPasswordOption)
        .addCredentialOption(getGoogleIdOption)
        .build()
}

private fun registerWithGoogleRequest(): GetCredentialRequest {
    val signInRequestOptions = GetGoogleIdOption.Builder().setFilterByAuthorizedAccounts(false)
        .setServerClientId(Config.WEB_CLIENT_ID).setAutoSelectEnabled(false).build()
    return GetCredentialRequest.Builder().addCredentialOption(signInRequestOptions).build()
}

The sign-in request includes saved passwords and filters Google choices to previously authorized accounts. The registration request removes that Google-account filter. This controls which credentials Credential Manager offers, not whether a Firebase user already exists. Both Google paths pass the selected token to FirebaseAuth.signInWithCredential, which can create a Firebase user on first successful sign-in. Email/password registration instead calls createUserWithEmailAndPassword explicitly.

See the Credential Manager account-filter contract and Firebase's first-sign-in behavior. For a first Google authorization, use the app's registration flow; the sign-in request does not implement an automatic retry with the filter disabled.

docs.title: Firestore Security Rules
docs.text:
Sync (firebase/firestore/.../FirebaseDataSourceImpl.kt) writes to /dev.atick.jetpack/{userId}/jetpacks/{jetpackId}, one document per FirebaseJetpack (id, name, price, userId, lastUpdated, lastSynced, serverUpdatedAt, deleted — 8 fields). The mapper leaves serverUpdatedAt null on writes so Firestore assigns a server timestamp. See Data for the sync algorithm. Review this example under Firestore Database → Rules, test it, and explicitly Publish it for your project:

rules_version = '2';
service cloud.firestore {
  match /databases/{database}/documents {
    function isUserOwner(userId) {
      return request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == userId;
    }

    function isValidJetpack(jetpack) {
      return jetpack.size() == 8
        && jetpack.id is string
        && jetpack.name is string
        && jetpack.price is number
        && jetpack.userId is string
        && jetpack.lastUpdated is number
        && jetpack.lastSynced is number
        && jetpack.deleted is bool
        // Require the timestamp assigned by Firestore for this write.
        && jetpack.serverUpdatedAt == request.time;
    }

    match /dev.atick.jetpack/{userId}/jetpacks/{jetpackId} {
      allow read: if isUserOwner(userId);
      allow create: if isUserOwner(userId) && isValidJetpack(request.resource.data);
      allow update: if isUserOwner(userId) && isValidJetpack(request.resource.data)
        && request.resource.data.id == resource.data.id;
      allow delete: if isUserOwner(userId);
    }

    match /{document=**} {
      allow read, write: if false;
    }
  }
}

Editing this Markdown example does not deploy rules. Use the Rules Playground to check an owner's read/create/update/delete requests and denied unauthenticated or other-user requests before publishing. A rule that deploys successfully can still deny the app's requests at runtime. The example checks ownership by path and the stated field shape; assess any additional application validation before using it beyond this demonstration.

docs.title: Deploy rules from the CLI
docs.text:
The repository tracks a deployable rule set in firestore.rules, and firebase.json points the Firebase CLI at it:

npm install -g firebase-tools   # once
firebase login                  # once
firebase deploy --only firestore:rules --project <your-project-id>

firestore.rules differs from the example above. It is a transitional set for projects that still have pre-2.0.0 installs (see Existing installs and documents): it also accepts the older 7-field shape, and it requires a non-negative price. A new project with no older installs can replace its contents with the example above before deploying.

Nothing deploys rules automatically: not CI, not CD, not the Gradle build. No .firebaserc is tracked, because each adopter uses their own project; pass --project, or run firebase use --add to create one locally.

Deletion is soft in local Room data, then sync calls Firestore's hard-delete operation. It does not publish a tombstone: another device's existing local copy is not removed by the incremental query merely because the remote document is absent.

docs.title: Existing installs and documents
docs.text:
Warning

Version 2.0.0 changes Room schema 1 → 2 without a migration and enables destructive fallback. Upgrading an existing install can erase local rows, including edits or deletions not yet uploaded. Re-fetching remote data cannot restore changes that never reached the server.

The new pull query filters on serverUpdatedAt; legacy documents missing that field are excluded, even on a first pull with a zero cursor. The eight-field example rules also reject older writers that omit that timestamp.

For the rules side of a rollout, the tracked firestore.rules accepts both shapes. Publish it before releasing, so pre-2.0.0 clients keep writing while the update rolls out. Remove its isLegacyJetpack branch once no older installs remain. Legacy documents it accepts still lack serverUpdatedAt, so new clients never pull them. Making them visible needs a backfill, which this guide does not supply; do not assume an existing dataset can be upgraded by replacing configuration files alone.

docs.title: Verify a configured project
docs.text:
1. Rebuild after setting the JSON and web client ID. Register a Google account through the app, or register with email/password, and confirm the user appears in Firebase Authentication.

  2. With network access, add an item and check for a document at dev.atick.jetpack/{Firebase user UID}/jetpacks/{item ID} in Firestore. Edit it and confirm the document changes. Local UI updates alone do not prove a successful remote write.

  3. Delete the test item and confirm the document is removed remotely. This checks the current single-client path, not cross-device delete propagation or conflict handling.

  4. If requests fail, check provider enablement, application ID, the tested build's fingerprint, web client ID, and published rules. Use Troubleshooting for diagnostics.

The sync implementation has known concurrency and delivery limitations; these smoke checks do not establish lossless synchronization. See Data for the current implementation.

docs.title: Crashlytics
docs.text:
firebase:analytics exposes CrashReporter, implemented by FirebaseCrashReporter, which forwards non-fatal exceptions to FirebaseCrashlytics.recordException. The app applies FirebaseConventionPlugin, which enables Google Services and Crashlytics plugins and adds the Analytics, Crashlytics, and Performance SDKs. No custom Analytics event API or Performance trace instrumentation is implemented here, and the Performance Gradle plugin is not applied. See the official Analytics and Performance Monitoring guides for SDK-provided collection and the setup required for additional instrumentation.

For your configured Firebase app, follow the console's Crashlytics onboarding and the official test procedure. In a disposable debug test, trigger a deliberate uncaught exception, then restart the app so it can send the crash report. Remove temporary crash code afterward. To exercise the wrapper instead, call reportException and inspect non-fatal reports. If a test crash is still absent after five minutes, use the official debug-logging instructions to check configuration and upload errors; delay alone does not identify the cause.

Release builds enable R8 minification. The applied Crashlytics plugin enables mapping-file upload by default for obfuscated variants; this project does not override mappingFileUploadEnabled. Successful upload still depends on a configured app and access to Firebase. See readable crash reports for mapping-upload settings and Build & Tooling for CI configuration.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide gets the project running on your machine: clone, build the debug variant, then optionally configure Firebase and release signing.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Android Studio Quail 2 (2026.1.2), or a later release supporting AGP 9.3. Check the official compatibility table before choosing an IDE; this project pins AGP 9.3.1.
  • JDK 21 for both Android Studio's Gradle JDK and command-line builds (JAVA_HOME). Check the command-line runtime with ./gradlew --version after cloning.
  • Android SDK Platform 37 (the project's compileSdk) and Android SDK Platform-Tools, installed through Android Studio's SDK Manager. Accept the SDK licenses when prompted.
  • An Android device or emulator running API 24 (Android 7.0) or higher. Use an emulator image with Google Play services when testing Google Sign-In.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
1. Clone and enter the checkout:

    git clone --depth 1 -b main https://github.com/atick-faisal/Jetpack-Android-Starter.git
cd Jetpack-Android-Starter

  2. Open the checkout in Android Studio, select JDK 21 as the Gradle JDK, and let Gradle sync. Studio records your SDK location in ignored local.properties. For command-line-only setup, create that file with sdk.dir=/absolute/path/to/Android/sdk for your SDK installation.

  3. Build the debug variant:

    ./gradlew assembleDebug

    The APK is written to app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk.

  4. Start an emulator, or connect a device with USB debugging enabled and authorize the computer. Select it in Android Studio and run the app configuration. Alternatively, with one device connected, install from the terminal:

    ./gradlew installDebug

    Then open Jetpack from the device's launcher. Installation alone does not launch the app.

The tracked template google-services.json allows a fresh checkout to build and open the app. Authentication and remote sync require your own Firebase project; a successful build does not verify access to those services. Follow the setup below before testing sign-in and Firestore.

docs.title: Setting Up Firebase Features
docs.text:
This project includes Firebase integration for authentication, Firestore, and crash reporting. The app also includes Analytics and Performance SDK dependencies; see the Firebase guide for the configured scope.

Note

For complete setup instructions, see the Firebase Setup Guide. It covers creating your Firebase project, configuring Authentication (Google Sign-In and Email/Password), setting up Firestore, and downloading google-services.json.

docs.title: Release Build Setup
docs.text:
Create a keystore file using Android Studio's "Generate Signed Bundle/APK" tool, then place it in the app/ directory. Create keystore.properties in the project root:

storePassword=your-store-password
keyPassword=your-key-password
keyAlias=your-key-alias
storeFile=your-keystore-file.jks

storeFile is resolved relative to app/, so the example names a file directly inside that directory. These values are placeholders; use your own signing credentials.

Build the release variant:

./gradlew assembleRelease

Caution

If keystore.properties is missing, app/build.gradle.kts does not fail the build — it silently signs the release variant with the debug key, warning only via a println that's easy to miss in build output. A debug-signed release APK can be installed, but Google Play rejects debug-signed uploads. Switching to a different signing certificate normally prevents an in-place update of an installed app; keep the same signing identity for updates. Uninstalling to change certificates removes app data. Never commit keystore.properties, the keystore file, or your real google-services.json.

docs.title: Adding a Feature
docs.text:
This walks through adding a feature end to end, using the home feature (Jetpack library cards — a list screen plus a create/edit screen) as the running example, because it's the only feature in the repo that touches every layer: a Room-backed local store, an offline-first repository with two-way Firebase sync, two ViewModels, and two Navigation 3 destinations.

Use the excerpts to understand the existing wiring, then follow the For your feature steps to add your own model and screens. Existing Home code is already registered: do not paste a second copy of its bindings, entities, or entries into this checkout. Code marked “excerpt” omits imports or members and is not a complete file; the worked test below is a complete file.

Start with Getting Started and a working debug build. This walkthrough uses existing dependencies and plugins. Adding a new module or dependency is a separate approval decision in this repository; documenting its setup does not authorize changing the production module graph.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Module setup — existing screen or approved new module
  • Data models — domain model + persistence model
  • Data source — Room-backed local access
  • Repository — the offline-first contract the UI depends on
  • UI layer — ViewModel + screen
  • Navigation — NavKeys and entries
  • Dependency injection — wiring it all together

docs.title: Module setup
docs.text:
If the screen belongs to an existing feature, add its screen/ViewModel under feature/<feature>/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/feature/<feature>/ui/<screen>/ and register its key in that feature's navigation/ file. No new Gradle module or app dependency is needed.

For an approved new Compose feature module, create feature/<feature>/build.gradle.kts. The following is the complete build script for existing :feature:home; substitute your module's namespace:

plugins {
    alias(libs.plugins.jetpack.ui.library)
    alias(libs.plugins.jetpack.dagger.hilt)
    alias(libs.plugins.jetpack.dokka)
}

android {
    namespace = "dev.atick.feature.home"
}

dependencies {
    implementation(projects.core.ui)
    implementation(projects.data)
    testImplementation(projects.core.testing)
}
  1. Add include(":feature:<feature>") to root settings.gradle.kts beside the other features.
  2. Add implementation(projects.feature.<feature>) to app/build.gradle.kts. Gradle generates this accessor from the included module path; use a simple lower-case module name.
  3. Create src/main/AndroidManifest.xml containing <manifest />. Place Kotlin files under src/main/kotlin/, resources under src/main/res/, and unit tests under src/test/kotlin/.
  4. Prefix every library resource with the module path: :feature:catalog uses feature_catalog_. Update R imports and resource references when adapting another feature's screens. App resources use the app's own R, not the feature's generated R.

core:ui exports Compose, Navigation 3, Navigator, and Hilt's Compose ViewModel API. The existing plugins configure serialization and Hilt/KSP; do not add versions or duplicate compiler plugins. Features access persistence through :data, without a direct dependency on Room, Firebase, or another feature. See Build & Tooling for plugin responsibilities.

Source locations below abbreviate the package root: data/model/ means data/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/data/model/, and core/room/data/ means core/room/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/core/room/data/. Feature Kotlin files similarly live below feature/<feature>/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/feature/<feature>/.

docs.title: 1. Data models
docs.text:
Two models, not one: a Room @Entity for storage, and a plain domain model the rest of the app depends on. Extension functions map between them (and, for home, a third — FirebaseJetpack — for the Firestore side of the sync).

// Existing entity excerpt; imports and comments omitted.
@Entity(tableName = "jetpacks")
data class JetpackEntity(
    @PrimaryKey val id: String = UUID.randomUUID().toString(),
    val name: String,
    val price: Double,
    val userId: String = String(),
    val lastUpdated: Long = 0,
    val lastSynced: Long = 0,
    val serverUpdatedAtNanos: Long = 0,
    val needsSync: Boolean = false,
    val deleted: Boolean = false,
    val syncAction: SyncAction = SyncAction.NONE,
)

// Existing model/mapping excerpt; imports and remaining mapping arguments omitted.
data class Jetpack(
    val id: String = UUID.randomUUID().toString(),
    val name: String = String(),
    val price: Double = 0.0,
    val lastUpdated: Long = System.currentTimeMillis(),
    val lastSynced: Long = 0L,
    val needsSync: Boolean = true,
    val formattedDate: String = lastUpdated.asFormattedDateTime(),
)

fun JetpackEntity.toJetpack(): Jetpack = Jetpack(id = id, name = name, price = price, /* ... */)
fun Jetpack.toJetpackEntity(): JetpackEntity = JetpackEntity(id = id, name = name, price = price, /* ... */)

Note

lastUpdated orders Home's list and participates in pending-row selection; lastSynced, serverUpdatedAtNanos, needsSync, deleted, and syncAction support its sync/delete behavior. A local-only feature can omit remote bookkeeping and implement its own deletion policy.

For your feature: put the public model in data/model/<feature>/ and the Room entity in core/room/model/. Add explicit mapping functions in the data model package; carry every field your repository needs. For a synced feature, also define its remote DTO in firebase/firestore/model/ and mappings in :data. Home's complete mappings are in data/model/home/Jetpack.kt; do not use an abbreviated constructor above as a complete sync mapping. The two-clock and mapping reference explains the timestamps.

docs.title: 2. Data source
docs.text:
LocalDataSource wraps the Room DAO and moves every call onto IoDispatcher:

// Existing implementation excerpt; imports and other members omitted.
internal class LocalDataSourceImpl @Inject constructor(
    private val jetpackDao: JetpackDao,
    @IoDispatcher private val ioDispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher,
) : LocalDataSource {
    override fun getJetpacks(userId: String): Flow<List<JetpackEntity>> =
        jetpackDao.getJetpacks(userId).flowOn(ioDispatcher)

    override suspend fun upsertJetpack(jetpackEntity: JetpackEntity) = withContext(ioDispatcher) {
        jetpackDao.upsertJetpack(jetpackEntity)
    }
    // ...
}

Note

home's remote counterpart is Firestore, reached through FirebaseDataSource — see firebase/firestore. core:network also ships a NetworkDataSource/JetpackRestApi pair, but HomeRepositoryImpl doesn't use it; it's there for a feature that talks to a plain REST backend instead of Firestore. Use whichever remote your feature actually needs — not both.

docs.title: Register persistence before injecting it
docs.text:
For your feature, extend :core:room in this order:

  1. Add a @Dao in core/room/data/ with the observed read queries and suspend writes your feature needs. Home's JetpackDao.getJetpacks(userId) filters owner and soft-deleted rows; its getJetpack(id) filters only ID. Choose and test ownership/missing-row behavior explicitly rather than assuming every Home query is owner-scoped.
  2. Add the entity to JetpackDatabase's @Database(entities = [...]) and an abstract DAO accessor. This database lives in core/room/data/JetpackDatabase.kt.
  3. Add a provider to core/room/di/DaoModule.kt. The existing provider is shown below; for a new DAO, change both the return type and database accessor.
  4. Add your read/write methods to LocalDataSource and implement them in LocalDataSourceImpl. Inject the new DAO into that implementation. Use flowOn(ioDispatcher) for upstream Flow work and withContext(ioDispatcher) for suspend writes, following the existing methods.
  5. Keep the existing LocalDataSource binding; adding methods does not require another binding. If introducing a separate data-source interface, add its constructor-injected implementation and a binding in DataSourceModule, following Dependency injection.
// Existing DaoModule excerpt; imports and other providers omitted.
@Module(includes = [DatabaseModule::class])
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object DaoModule {
    @Singleton
    @Provides
    fun provideJetpackDao(jetpackDatabase: JetpackDatabase): JetpackDao =
        jetpackDatabase.getJetpackDao()
}

Changing the entity list changes the database schema. For existing installations, increment the version and register/test a data-preserving migration before release. The current database is version 2 with destructive fallback and no migration path; copying that fallback can erase pending local changes. Follow Room persistence and schema changes for schema export and migration testing. An in-memory test of the new schema does not test an upgrade.

docs.title: 3. Repository
docs.text:
Home ViewModels depend on a repository interface for data access. It returns Flow for observable reads and Result<Unit> for writes, via suspendRunCatching:

// Existing interface excerpt; imports omitted.
interface HomeRepository : Syncable {
    fun getJetpacks(): Flow<List<Jetpack>>
    fun getJetpack(id: String): Flow<Jetpack>
    suspend fun createOrUpdateJetpack(jetpack: Jetpack): Result<Unit>
    suspend fun markJetpackAsDeleted(jetpack: Jetpack): Result<Unit>
}

// Existing method excerpts; class, constructor, imports and other members omitted.
override fun getJetpacks(): Flow<List<Jetpack>> {
    syncManager.requestSync()
    return flow {
        val userId = preferencesDataSource.getUserIdOrThrow()
        emitAll(localDataSource.getJetpacks(userId).map { it.mapToJetpacks() })
    }
}

override suspend fun createOrUpdateJetpack(jetpack: Jetpack): Result<Unit> = suspendRunCatching {
    val userId = preferencesDataSource.getUserIdOrThrow()
    localDataSource.upsertJetpack(
        jetpack.toJetpackEntity().copy(
            userId = userId,
            lastUpdated = System.currentTimeMillis(),
            needsSync = true,
            syncAction = SyncAction.UPSERT,
        ),
    )
    syncManager.requestSync()
}

The UI observes Room; a successful write Result covers local persistence and the sync request, not confirmed remote delivery. HomeRepositoryImpl additionally implements sync(), which pushes unsynced entities to Firestore and pulls remote changes back — the full two-way algorithm is covered in Data Layer. A feature with no remote doesn't implement Syncable at all.

For your feature: add its interface and internal implementation under data/repository/<feature>/. Inject data sources with @Inject constructor, map entities to public models, and use suspendRunCatching for one-time operations. Bind the interface in data/di/RepositoryModule.kt. Keep I/O dispatch in data sources. For a local-only repository, omit Syncable, sync requests, and remote dependencies. For a REST-backed feature, follow the remote-source options; the existing Home repository does not use REST.

docs.title: Connect a synced feature to the worker
docs.text:
Syncable is a contract, not automatic discovery. sync/worker/SyncWorker.kt currently injects only HomeRepository and collects homeRepository.sync(). To add another synced repository after agreeing its sync behavior, inject it there and explicitly collect its sync Flow inside the worker's existing I/O/error-handling path. Define ordering and progress reporting across repositories; returning a Flow without collecting it performs no synchronization. Reuse the current SyncManager request path and worker delegation rather than creating a second scheduler incidentally.

Read Two-way sync before adapting the algorithm. Home takes one pending snapshot, has no guaranteed drain after writes during a pass, and can overwrite concurrent edits. It is not a conflict-resolution or reliable cross-device deletion protocol. New collections also need their own remote model, query, and reviewed security-rule setup.

docs.title: 4. UI layer
docs.text:
Home uses one ViewModel per screen, each exposing a StateFlow<UiState<ScreenData>>. Use an immutable screen-data class co-located with its ViewModel; Home's HomeScreenData has jetpacks: List<Jetpack> = emptyList(). The following existing class excerpt omits imports and the screen-data declaration. Its observation method maps the repository Flow, stores updates and errors in _homeUiState, then launches collection in viewModelScope:

// feature/home/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/feature/home/ui/home/HomeViewModel.kt
@HiltViewModel
class HomeViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val homeRepository: HomeRepository,
) : ViewModel() {
    private val _homeUiState = MutableStateFlow(UiState(HomeScreenData()))
    val homeUiState = _homeUiState
        .onStart { getJetpacks() }
        .stateInDelayed(UiState(HomeScreenData()), viewModelScope)

    private fun getJetpacks() {
        homeRepository.getJetpacks()
            .map(::HomeScreenData)
            .onEach { data -> _homeUiState.update { UiState(data) } }
            .catch { e -> _homeUiState.update { it.copy(error = e.asOneTimeEvent()) } }
            .launchIn(viewModelScope)
    }

    fun deleteJetpack(jetpack: Jetpack) {
        _homeUiState.updateWith { homeRepository.markJetpackAsDeleted(jetpack) }
    }
}

Observation limitation: Home and Item start ViewModel-owned repository jobs inside onStart. Resubscribing after the sharing timeout starts another job while the old one remains alive. Treat these excerpts as current wiring, not a subscription-lifetime solution; see Subscription lifetimes and the bounded Observation lifetime follow-up before adapting them.

The detail ViewModel handles both create and edit, taking the optional existing ID by assisted injection from its NavKey. This existing class excerpt omits imports, state declarations, and load/save methods; the complete factory-to-Screen chain is in Navigation:

// feature/home/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/feature/home/ui/item/ItemViewModel.kt
@HiltViewModel(assistedFactory = ItemViewModel.Factory::class)
class ItemViewModel @AssistedInject constructor(
    private val homeRepository: HomeRepository,
    @Assisted private val existingJetpackId: String?,
) : ViewModel() {

    @AssistedFactory
    interface Factory {
        fun create(existingJetpackId: String?): ItemViewModel
    }

    fun updateName(name: String) {
        _itemUiState.updateState { copy(jetpackName = name) }
    }

    // State declarations, updatePrice, loading and saving are omitted here.
}

Keep jetpackPrice as raw text in ItemScreenData; updatePrice stores it without parsing. Current save trims the name and parses the price once, with invalid/empty input becoming 0.0; this is not range validation. Define validation for the adopter's product separately.

Save/load limitation: current Item ignores the repository save Result and requests navigation even on failure. Its load error handler constructs a state without storing it. Do not copy those methods as successful persistence handling. The proposed save replacement maps the returned Result before requesting navigation; it remains a proposed change and does not fix load errors, concurrent edits, or event delivery. These runtime fixes remain separate from this walkthrough.

For your feature: co-locate <Name>Screen.kt and <Name>ViewModel.kt under ui/<screen>/. Expose immutable screen data through UiState, update inputs with updateState, and propagate returned Results through updateWith/updateStateWith. Provide explicit screen callbacks for item clicks, save, delete, and back; keep navigation in the composable/entry callback.

The screen collects that state and hands it to StatefulComposable, which renders loading/error around your content:

// Existing Screen excerpt; imports and the private content overload omitted.
@Composable
internal fun HomeScreen(
    onJetpackClick: (String) -> Unit,
    onShowSnackbar: suspend (String, SnackbarAction, Throwable?) -> Boolean,
    homeViewModel: HomeViewModel = hiltViewModel(),
) {
    val homeState by homeViewModel.homeUiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

    StatefulComposable(state = homeState, onShowSnackbar = onShowSnackbar) { homeScreenData ->
        HomeScreen(
            jetpacks = homeScreenData.jetpacks,
            onJetpackCLick = onJetpackClick,
            onDeleteJetpack = homeViewModel::deleteJetpack,
        )
    }
}

For the complete import list, use the existing screen in the source tree: collection is androidx.lifecycle.compose.collectAsStateWithLifecycle, Hilt creation is androidx.hilt.lifecycle.viewmodel.compose.hiltViewModel, and delegated Compose state uses androidx.compose.runtime.getValue. StatefulComposable and SnackbarAction are in dev.atick.core.ui.utils. Keep the injected destination screen internal; its public entry function is the boundary the app calls. A private content overload can support previews without introducing a separate Route destination.

Item's screen supplies itemId through the assisted factory described in Passing arguments to ViewModels. Inside its StatefulComposable content, it wires raw name/price state to updateName/updatePrice, save to createOrUpdateJetpack, and back to onBackClick. It consumes navigateBack in LaunchedEffect(screenData.navigateBack, onBackClick) and calls back only when consumed content is true. Consumption is not a guarantee of completed navigation; the existing snackbar event path also has delivery limitations.

UiState, the update helpers, and StatefulComposable contracts are covered in State Management.

docs.title: 5. Navigation
docs.text:
Each screen gets a @Serializable NavKey, a Navigator extension to reach it, and an entry registration:

// Existing navigation excerpt; package/imports and navigateToHome omitted.
@Serializable
data object HomeNavKey : NavKey

@Serializable
data class ItemNavKey(val itemId: String?) : NavKey

fun Navigator.navigateToItem(itemId: String?) = navigate(ItemNavKey(itemId))

fun EntryProviderScope<NavKey>.homeEntries(
    navigator: Navigator,
    onShowSnackbar: suspend (String, SnackbarAction, Throwable?) -> Boolean,
) {
    entry<HomeNavKey>(metadata = ListDetailSceneStrategy.listPane()) {
        HomeScreen(onJetpackClick = navigator::navigateToItem, onShowSnackbar = onShowSnackbar)
    }
    entry<ItemNavKey>(metadata = ListDetailSceneStrategy.detailPane()) { key ->
        ItemScreen(itemId = key.itemId, onBackClick = navigator::goBack, onShowSnackbar = onShowSnackbar)
    }
}

homeEntries(navigator, onShowSnackbar) is then called inside the app-level entryProvider { } in app/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/compose/ui/JetpackApp.kt. How NavKeys carry arguments into a ViewModel by assisted injection, and how the scene strategies decide list/detail layout, are covered in Navigation.

For your feature: create keys and a public EntryProviderScope<NavKey> registration function in feature/<feature>/navigation/. Use kotlinx.serialization.Serializable, androidx.navigation3.runtime.NavKey and EntryProviderScope, androidx.compose.material3.adaptive.navigation3.ListDetailSceneStrategy, and dev.atick.core.navigation.Navigator. Import your module's internal screens there. Register each key type once in the app's active entry provider and import the public registration function in JetpackApp.kt.

For a new tab, add an enum entry to app/.../navigation/TopLevelDestination.kt with selected/unselected icons, app string labels/title, and the new root key. Its keys property automatically includes enum entries. Keep START unchanged unless intentionally changing the exit/start destination. Registering an entry alone does not add a tab. For create, add an app callback using navigateToItem(null) (Home's FAB is in JetpackApp.kt); the list click passes the existing ID. Adapt the app's Home-specific FAB condition when adding another feature's create action. A nested-only screen needs neither a tab nor a new top-level key.

Preserve the existing entry decorators, scene strategy, and explicit back handler. See Navigation for tab restoration, identity constraints, and account-boundary behavior.

docs.title: 6. Dependency injection
docs.text:
The existing repository binding, including its containing module, is:

// Existing RepositoryModule excerpt; imports and unrelated bindings omitted.
@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
abstract class RepositoryModule {
    @Binds
    @Singleton
    internal abstract fun bindHomeRepository(
        homeRepositoryImpl: HomeRepositoryImpl,
    ): HomeRepository
}

Use dagger.Binds, dagger.Module, dagger.hilt.InstallIn, dagger.hilt.components.SingletonComponent, and javax.inject.Singleton. The implementation's constructor uses javax.inject.Inject. Add your binding to this existing module; do not create a second RepositoryModule with the same package/name.

core/room/di/DataSourceModule.kt has the same @Module/@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class) container and binds LocalDataSourceImpl to LocalDataSource. The database and DAO use @Provides because they need construction/accessor calls. Data sources inject the dispatcher with dev.atick.core.di.IoDispatcher; Data covers qualifiers and scopes.

The app already has @HiltAndroidApp on App and @AndroidEntryPoint on MainActivity. Do not create another application class when adding a feature. Annotate normal injected ViewModels with @HiltViewModel; an assisted ViewModel also needs its factory and the Screen's creationCallback. Adding @HiltViewModel alone does not supply runtime arguments.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
This complete test file exercises the existing Home ViewModel, whose delete method propagates returned Results correctly. Place HomeFeatureExampleTest.kt in feature/home/src/test/kotlin/dev/atick/feature/home/ui/home/ when trying the example. It starts active state collection, observes real fake-repository data, and suspends the write so loading is observable. It checks a successful operation and a returned failure without recommending Item's current failed-save behavior. No Hilt instrumentation graph is required.

package dev.atick.feature.home.ui.home

import androidx.lifecycle.viewModelScope
import app.cash.turbine.test
import com.google.common.truth.Truth.assertThat
import dev.atick.core.testing.rule.MainDispatcherRule
import dev.atick.data.model.home.Jetpack
import dev.atick.data.repository.home.HomeRepository
import dev.atick.data.utils.SyncProgress
import kotlinx.coroutines.CompletableDeferred
import kotlinx.coroutines.cancel
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.emptyFlow
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest
import org.junit.Rule
import org.junit.Test

class HomeFeatureExampleTest {
    @get:Rule
    val mainDispatcherRule = MainDispatcherRule()

    @Test
    fun `successful delete clears loading and updates the observed list`() = runTest {
        checkDelete(Result.success(Unit))
    }

    @Test
    fun `failed delete clears loading and preserves the item with an error`() = runTest {
        checkDelete(Result.failure(IllegalStateException("delete failed")))
    }

    private suspend fun checkDelete(result: Result<Unit>) {
        val item = Jetpack(id = "compose", name = "Compose")
        val repository = ExampleHomeRepository(item)
        val viewModel = HomeViewModel(repository)
        try {
            viewModel.homeUiState.test {
                var initial = awaitItem()
                while (initial.data.jetpacks.isEmpty()) initial = awaitItem()
                assertThat(initial.data.jetpacks).containsExactly(item)

                viewModel.deleteJetpack(item)
                assertThat(awaitItem().loading).isTrue()
                assertThat(repository.deletedId).isEqualTo(item.id)

                repository.completion.complete(result)
                val finished = expectMostRecentItem()
                assertThat(finished.loading).isFalse()
                assertThat(finished.error.peekContent()).isSameInstanceAs(result.exceptionOrNull())
                if (result.isSuccess) {
                    assertThat(finished.data.jetpacks).isEmpty()
                } else {
                    assertThat(finished.data.jetpacks).containsExactly(item)
                }
                cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()
            }
        } finally {
            viewModel.viewModelScope.cancel()
        }
    }
}

private class ExampleHomeRepository(item: Jetpack) : HomeRepository {
    private val items = MutableStateFlow(listOf(item))
    val completion = CompletableDeferred<Result<Unit>>()
    var deletedId: String? = null
        private set

    override fun getJetpacks(): Flow<List<Jetpack>> = items
    override fun getJetpack(id: String): Flow<Jetpack> =
        items.map { rows -> rows.first { it.id == id } }

    override suspend fun createOrUpdateJetpack(jetpack: Jetpack): Result<Unit> =
        Result.success(Unit)

    override suspend fun markJetpackAsDeleted(jetpack: Jetpack): Result<Unit> {
        deletedId = jetpack.id
        return completion.await().also { result ->
            if (result.isSuccess) items.value = items.value.filterNot { it.id == jetpack.id }
        }
    }

    override suspend fun sync(): Flow<SyncProgress> = emptyFlow()
}

MainDispatcherRule runs eagerly by default, which makes the completion assertions deterministic here. This is not an overlap/concurrency test. Adapt the fake to your own repository and assert its observable behavior, returned failures, and the exact fields persisted. The Item input example separately covers raw price text.

docs.title: Validate the integrated feature
docs.text:
Run from the repository root, substituting the module name for an approved new feature:

./gradlew :feature:home:testDebugUnitTest :core:navigation:testDebugUnitTest
./gradlew :core:room:testDebugUnitTest :data:testDebugUnitTest
./gradlew :app:assembleDebug
./gradlew spotlessCheck --init-script gradle/init.gradle.kts --no-configuration-cache

Add an in-memory Room DAO test for the new entity/query, following JetpackDaoTest, and a repository test with fake data sources covering mappings, local writes, and returned failures. Registering an entity without exercising its DAO is insufficient. A database upgrade additionally needs migration tests. Keep tests in their owning modules; constructor fakes need no @HiltAndroidTest setup.

On an emulator/device with Firebase configured, exercise list → create → save → edit → back, a failed write, and tab switching. Rotate/recreate while a detail is open; verify the right tab and arguments restore. Check narrow/wide layouts and back at both detail and top-level roots. Sign out and confirm back cannot expose the old graph; test account-specific data separately. These are manual acceptance checks, not claims that the JVM tests cover Firebase, remote sync, or UI rendering. For synced features, also test worker invocation, offline writes and later sync, and the concurrency cases in the sync limitations.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: This template uses Jetpack Navigation 3, not navigation-compose. There is no navigation graph resource, no route strings, and no back-stack argument bundle — destinations are typed keys, and a small core/navigation module owns the state and the one class allowed to change it.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: Type What it does Where NavKey Marker for a destination. @Serializable, so it survives process death. one per destination, next to its feature's entries (e.g. HomeNavKey, ItemNavKey) NavigationState Holds one back stack per top-level destination, plus the order they were visited in. core/navigation/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/core/navigation/NavigationState.kt Navigator The only thing that mutates NavigationState. core/navigation/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/core/navigation/Navigator.kt NavDisplay Renders the flattened back stack. app/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/compose/ui/JetpackApp.kt entry<T> / entryProvider Maps a NavKey type to a composable. per-feature navigation/*Navigation.kt files ListDetailSceneStrategy Adaptive list/detail layout for wide windows. JetpackApp.kt, feature/home/.../navigation/HomeNavigation.kt

docs.title: Defining a destination
docs.text:
A destination with no argument is a data object; one with an argument is a data class:

// feature/auth/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/feature/auth/navigation/AuthNavigation.kt
@Serializable
data object SignInNavKey : NavKey

// feature/home/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/feature/home/navigation/HomeNavigation.kt
@Serializable
data class ItemNavKey(val itemId: String?) : NavKey

docs.title: Registering entries
docs.text:
Each feature module exposes an EntryProviderScope<NavKey> extension that registers its destinations. Metadata (like ListDetailSceneStrategy.listPane()) attaches per entry, not per graph:

// feature/home/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/feature/home/navigation/HomeNavigation.kt
fun EntryProviderScope<NavKey>.homeEntries(
    navigator: Navigator,
    onShowSnackbar: suspend (String, SnackbarAction, Throwable?) -> Boolean,
) {
    entry<HomeNavKey>(
        metadata = ListDetailSceneStrategy.listPane(),
    ) {
        HomeScreen(
            onJetpackClick = navigator::navigateToItem,
            onShowSnackbar = onShowSnackbar,
        )
    }

    entry<ItemNavKey>(
        metadata = ListDetailSceneStrategy.detailPane(),
    ) { key ->
        ItemScreen(
            itemId = key.itemId,
            onBackClick = navigator::goBack,
            onShowSnackbar = onShowSnackbar,
        )
    }
}

The app module combines each feature's entries under one entryProvider { } per graph (see Wiring NavDisplay). Each feature also declares fun Navigator.navigateToX() extensions next to its keys, so the app can wire callbacks through that feature's public API. A feature should not depend on another feature to call its extension; cross-feature wiring belongs in the app:

fun Navigator.navigateToItem(itemId: String?) = navigate(ItemNavKey(itemId))

docs.title: Multi-back-stack state
docs.text:
rememberNavigationState builds one back stack per top-level destination (subStacks) plus a separate stack recording the order those destinations were visited (topLevelStack):

// core/navigation/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/core/navigation/NavigationState.kt
@Composable
fun rememberNavigationState(
    startKey: NavKey,
    topLevelKeys: Set<NavKey>,
): NavigationState {
    val topLevelStack = rememberNavBackStack(startKey)

    val subStacks = topLevelKeys.associateWith { topLevelKey ->
        key(topLevelKey) { rememberNavBackStack(topLevelKey) }
    }

    return remember(startKey, topLevelKeys) {
        NavigationState(
            startKey = startKey,
            topLevelStack = topLevelStack,
            subStacks = subStacks,
        )
    }
}

Tip

key(topLevelKey) is what gives each sub stack its own saved-state slot. Without it, every iteration of the associateWith lambda shares the composition's compound key hash, so all the stacks register under one key and are restored by position rather than by which destination they belong to — a tab can silently come back with another tab's history after process death. NavigationStateTest (see Testing) is the regression test for this.

NavigationState derives the current tab and current screen from those two stacks, and never mutates itself — only Navigator does:

class NavigationState(
    val startKey: NavKey,
    val topLevelStack: NavBackStack<NavKey>,
    val subStacks: Map<NavKey, NavBackStack<NavKey>>,
) {
    val currentTopLevelKey: NavKey by derivedStateOf { topLevelStack.last() }
    val topLevelKeys: Set<NavKey> get() = subStacks.keys
    val currentSubStack: NavBackStack<NavKey>
        get() = subStacks[currentTopLevelKey]
            ?: error("Sub stack for $currentTopLevelKey does not exist")
    val currentKey: NavKey by derivedStateOf { currentSubStack.last() }
}

NavDisplay needs one flat list, not a map of stacks — the backStack extension property flattens them in visit order, which is also what makes back-from-another-tab return to the start tab rather than exiting the app:

val NavigationState.backStack: List<NavKey>
    get() = topLevelStack.flatMap { subStacks[it].orEmpty() }

docs.title: The Navigator
docs.text:
navigate(key) picks its behavior from what kind of destination key is:

key is... Effect the current top-level destination pops its stack back to the root — "tap the selected tab again to go home" another top-level destination switches to it, preserving where the user was anything else pushes onto the current top-level destination's stack 
// core/navigation/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/core/navigation/Navigator.kt
fun navigate(key: NavKey) {
    when (key) {
        state.currentTopLevelKey -> clearSubStack()
        in state.topLevelKeys -> goToTopLevel(key)
        else -> goToKey(key)
    }
}

fun goBack() {
    when (state.currentKey) {
        state.startKey -> Unit
        state.currentTopLevelKey -> state.topLevelStack.removeLastOrNull()
        else -> state.currentSubStack.removeLastOrNull()
    }
}

fun canGoBack(): Boolean = state.currentKey != state.startKey

Calling goBack() from the start key does nothing — there is nowhere left to go, and only the system back handler finishes the activity. A screen can wire a back button straight to navigator::goBack; use canGoBack() to decide whether to handle back at all (see Wiring NavDisplay).

docs.title: Entry identity and duplicate destinations
docs.text:
Two identities matter in this template:

  • Navigator uses key equality when removing a destination from the current sub-stack before pushing it. ItemNavKey("a") and ItemNavKey("b") are different keys; navigating to "a" again moves that key to the top of this sub-stack. It does not remove an equal key from another tab.
  • Navigation 3's entry decorators use NavEntry.contentKey. In the pinned Navigation 3 1.1.4, its default is key.toString(), not the key object. The saveable-state decorator passes this value to SaveableStateProvider; lifecycle 2.11.0 uses it to select the ViewModel store owner.

For these data-class keys, different item IDs produce different default content keys. Sharing a key type is therefore not itself a collision. Equal keys in two flattened tab stacks do collide; even unequal custom keys can collide if their toString() values are the same. The decorators associate state by content key, and simultaneous rendering of duplicate saveable-state keys can fail rather than produce two independent screens. The resolved Compose saveable-state 1.11.4 sources contain the duplicate-key check.

Keep a nested destination owned by one top-level stack when following the existing design. If two tabs need independent instances of a shared screen, give them distinct destination keys (separate key types are one option) and verify their content keys differ. Do not resolve this by overriding toString() casually: identity must stay stable across restoration. An owner argument or custom content-key policy requires a separately reviewed navigation design and restoration tests.

The version-specific behavior above was checked in the published Navigation 3 runtime sources and lifecycle decorator sources. Recheck this behavior when upgrading those dependencies.

docs.title: Wiring NavDisplay
docs.text:
JetpackApp picks between two independent graphs based on appState.isUserLoggedIn. Each graph builds its own NavigationState. Changing between signed-in and signed-out UI removes the previous graph's composition; back in the new graph does not traverse the removed graph's navigation history:

Graph Composable startKey topLevelKeys Signed-out SignedOutNavigation SignInNavKey setOf(SignInNavKey) Signed-in SignedInNavigation TopLevelDestination.START.key TopLevelDestination.keys

These are navigation boundaries, not data authorization or a complete account-reset protocol. A direct account change that leaves isUserLoggedIn true does not itself select another graph. Repositories, cached preferences and pending sync work need their own account handling.

The signed-in setup uses the enum's keys; the signed-out setup supplies SignInNavKey instead:

val navigationState = rememberNavigationState(
    startKey = TopLevelDestination.START.key,
    topLevelKeys = TopLevelDestination.keys,
)
val navigator = remember(navigationState) { Navigator(navigationState) }

NavDisplay renders the flattened backStack, and each entry gets its saved state and ViewModelStore from rememberDefaultEntryDecorators():

// app/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/compose/ui/JetpackApp.kt
NavDisplay(
    backStack = navigationState.backStack,
    entryDecorators = rememberDefaultEntryDecorators(),
    sceneStrategies = listOf(rememberListDetailSceneStrategy<NavKey>()),
    onBack = navigator::goBack,
    entryProvider = entryProvider {
        homeEntries(navigator, onShowSnackbar)
        profileEntries(onShowSnackbar)
    },
)

entryDecorators comes from core/navigation:

@Composable
fun rememberDefaultEntryDecorators(): List<NavEntryDecorator<NavKey>> = listOf(
    rememberSaveableStateHolderNavEntryDecorator(),
    rememberViewModelStoreNavEntryDecorator(),
)

NavDisplay installs its own back handler, but only while the current scene has entries behind it. The two-pane list-detail scene (see below) has the list and detail as one scene with nothing behind it, so the app also wires an explicit handler next to every NavDisplay:

BackHandler(enabled = navigator.canGoBack()) { navigator.goBack() }

docs.title: Add a destination to the app
docs.text:
1. Add the approved feature module as an app dependency, or keep the destination in its existing feature module. Expose its keys and entry-registration function publicly; the Screen can remain internal because the registration function calls it within that module.
  2. Import and call that registration function inside the appropriate entryProvider in JetpackApp.kt: signed-out for authentication, signed-in for authenticated screens. Every key that can be pushed in that graph needs a matching entry. Do not register one key type twice.
  3. For a tab, add an entry to app/.../navigation/TopLevelDestination.kt with its root key, selected and unselected icons, and app string resources for label/title. keys derives from enum entries; bar/rail items iterate those entries. Keep START pointing at the intended exit destination.
  4. Wire list clicks to the feature's navigator extension with an ID, and a create action with null if following Item's create/edit convention. Home's create FAB is explicitly conditional on the current top-level key in JetpackApp.kt; another tab's create action needs its own condition and callback. Registering a tab does not supply that action automatically.
  5. Preserve the existing decorators, scene strategy and explicit BackHandler. Verify switching tabs preserves each sub-stack, selecting the current tab pops to its root, and back from another tab's root follows top-level history. Returning to the start tab clears that history; back at the start key is left to the system.

A screen pushed only inside a tab does not need a TopLevelDestination enum entry. Follow the feature guide for model, DI, resources, and testing steps.

docs.title: Adaptive list-detail
docs.text:
The signed-in NavDisplay installs rememberListDetailSceneStrategy<NavKey>(). An entry opts into it with pane metadata — HomeNavKey is the list pane, ItemNavKey is the detail pane (both registered in homeEntries, shown under Registering entries). On a wide window the two render side by side; on a phone they behave as separate screens, and which layout applies is decided entirely by the scene strategy, not by the entries themselves.

One consequence: on a wide window the list pane is still on screen beside the detail, but the last key in the back stack is the detail key. JetpackApp.kt tracks this explicitly rather than guessing from window size, since guessing wrong stacks two top app bars on what should be a single full-screen destination:

val isAtTopLevel = navigationState.currentKey == navigationState.currentTopLevelKey

docs.title: Passing arguments to ViewModels
docs.text:
This template carries destination arguments on the NavKey itself and explicitly supplies them to the factory; it does not decode those arguments from a SavedStateHandle. The argument reaches the ViewModel through Hilt's assisted-injection support, using ItemNavKey.itemId as the example end to end:

  1. The key carries the argument: 
    data class ItemNavKey(val itemId: String?) : NavKey
  2. The entry reads it off the key and passes it to the composable: 
    entry<ItemNavKey>(metadata = ListDetailSceneStrategy.detailPane()) { key ->
    ItemScreen(itemId = key.itemId, onBackClick = navigator::goBack, onShowSnackbar = onShowSnackbar)
}
  3. The composable requests the ViewModel with a creationCallback: 
    // feature/home/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/feature/home/ui/item/ItemScreen.kt
itemViewModel: ItemViewModel = hiltViewModel<ItemViewModel, ItemViewModel.Factory>(
    creationCallback = { factory -> factory.create(itemId) },
),
  4. The ViewModel takes the argument through an @AssistedInject constructor: 
    // feature/home/src/main/kotlin/dev/atick/feature/home/ui/item/ItemViewModel.kt
@HiltViewModel(assistedFactory = ItemViewModel.Factory::class)
class ItemViewModel @AssistedInject constructor(
    private val homeRepository: HomeRepository,
    @Assisted private val existingJetpackId: String?,
) : ViewModel() {

    @AssistedFactory
    interface Factory {
        fun create(existingJetpackId: String?): ItemViewModel
    }
    // ...
}

Use kotlinx.serialization.Serializable on the real key declaration (as shown under Defining a destination); the abbreviated declaration in step 1 omits it. The Screen uses androidx.hilt.lifecycle.viewmodel.compose.hiltViewModel; factory annotations come from dagger.assisted, and HiltViewModel from dagger.hilt.android.lifecycle.

Every destination that needs a keyed argument in its ViewModel follows this four-step chain. The entry's ViewModel store retains an existing ViewModel; the creation callback supplies arguments when that instance is first created. It is not a mechanism for updating an existing ViewModel's arguments. Put identity-bearing arguments on the key and test restoration with two different IDs.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
core/navigation's own test suite covers this module directly — NavigatorTest builds a NavigationState by hand and exercises navigate()/goBack()'s branches, while NavigationStateTest drives an actual save/restore cycle with StateRestorationTester to guard the key() behavior described under Multi-back-stack state. See core/navigation/src/test/kotlin/dev/atick/core/navigation/ for both. Run:

./gradlew :core:navigation:testDebugUnitTest :feature:home:testDebugUnitTest

When adding a destination, test equal-key re-navigation, distinct argument keys, top-level history, and restoration. If extending cross-tab identity, include a real decorated NavDisplay test; NavigatorTest alone does not exercise saveable-state or ViewModel-store collisions. On a device, check system and toolbar back in narrow/wide layouts and sign-in/sign-out graph changes.

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: Screens expose StateFlow<UiState<ScreenData>> from their ViewModels and collect it with collectAsStateWithLifecycle() inside the destination's Screen composable. UiState keeps data, loading, and an error event together. The helpers handle common Result-returning operations, with important boundaries around exceptions, concurrent calls, and event delivery described below.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
API Purpose UiState<T> Current data, a loading flag, and OneTimeEvent<Throwable?> for an error StatefulComposable Renders data, a loading indicator, and an error callback updateState Synchronously replaces data while preserving loading and error updateStateWith Launches an operation returning Result<T> and replaces data on success updateWith Launches an operation returning Result<Unit> without replacing data OneTimeEvent<T> Allows at-most-once consumption per wrapper instance

The state helpers and wrapper live in core/ui/.../utils/StatefulComposable.kt; the event wrapper lives in core/android/.../utils/OneTimeEvent.kt.

docs.title: The UiState<T> wrapper
docs.text:
data class UiState<T : Any>(
    val data: T,
    val loading: Boolean = false,
    val error: OneTimeEvent<Throwable?> = OneTimeEvent(null),
)

Data remains present during loading and after a returned failure. Start with values the screen can render: HomeScreenData uses an empty list, while ItemScreenData uses empty name/price strings and a generated ID for a new item. A non-null data container does not prohibit nullable fields. Use null when absence is meaningful, and make the UI handle that case.

The wrapper's properties are read-only, but an event's consumed flag is mutable. Copying a UiState without replacing error retains the same event and its consumption state. Separate flows or custom state types can be appropriate for independently observed concerns; this wrapper is a shared default.

StatefulComposable renders content even while loading and adds a centered loading indicator. It consumes an error and attempts to call onShowSnackbar(message, SnackbarAction.REPORT, error); the callback's Boolean return is ignored. It does not implement retry or guarantee that the snackbar is displayed. See event delivery before relying on it for critical acknowledgement.

docs.title: Update functions
docs.text:
Function Use when Replaces data? Async? updateState Form edits and toggles Yes No updateStateWith An operation returns new screen data On returned success Yes updateWith An action returns no new data No Yes

The async helpers return Unit, not the operation's Result or a Job. Map the result inside the operation when success must change screen data. They use the context ViewModel's scope; they do not choose an IO dispatcher. Repository/data-source code owns the relevant dispatcher boundary.

docs.title: updateState
docs.text:
These are actual Item form methods:

fun updateName(name: String) {
    _itemUiState.updateState { copy(jetpackName = name) }
}

fun updatePrice(priceString: String) {
    _itemUiState.updateState { copy(jetpackPrice = priceString) }
}

The lambda returns replacement data. Loading and the existing error event remain unchanged. Because it uses MutableStateFlow.update, the transform can be evaluated again under contention: keep side effects out of it. Thrown exceptions propagate to the caller.

Keep the price as raw text so clearing it, entering 12e, or typing 1. preserves the exact input. "1.".toDoubleOrNull() accepts the trailing decimal point, but converting the result back to text would normalize it to "1.0". Preserving input and accepting a parsed number are different concerns. At save, Item trims the text and calls toDoubleOrNull() ?: 0.0. Empty or unparseable text becomes zero; this is fallback behavior, not price validation. No non-negative-price validation is present.

docs.title: updateStateWith
docs.text:
Starting the coroutine sets loading and replaces the old error with OneTimeEvent(null). A returned success replaces data and clears loading. A returned failure stores its throwable in a new event, preserves the current data, and clears loading. The implementation also rejects a successful null payload, although T : Any excludes null in ordinary typed calls.

Current Item limitation: createOrUpdateJetpack() ignores the repository's Result and returns success with navigateBack = OneTimeEvent(true). A failed repository save therefore still requests navigation and exposes no error. Its load catch also constructs a state without storing it, leaving the default form without a load error. These behaviors are covered by characterization tests and tracked under Item failure handling.

The following is a proposed replacement for the save method inside ItemViewModel, not the current implementation. It uses existing imports and APIs and maps a returned repository failure through to the helper:

fun createOrUpdateJetpack() {
    _itemUiState.updateStateWith {
        val jetpack = Jetpack(
            id = jetpackId,
            name = jetpackName.trim(),
            price = jetpackPrice.trim().toDoubleOrNull() ?: 0.0,
        )
        homeRepository.createOrUpdateJetpack(jetpack).map {
            copy(navigateBack = OneTimeEvent(true))
        }
    }
}

This addresses returned save failures only. It does not fix load errors, thrown exceptions, event delivery, or edits made during suspension. Repository success concerns local persistence and the sync-request boundary, not confirmed remote synchronization; see Data.

docs.title: updateWith
docs.text:
Home deletes an item through a Result-returning repository operation:

fun deleteJetpack(jetpack: Jetpack) {
    _homeUiState.updateWith {
        homeRepository.markJetpackAsDeleted(jetpack)
    }
}

This helper has the same loading/error setup and returned-failure handling as updateStateWith, but does not replace data on completion. Data changes instead arrive through the repository Flow.

docs.title: Exceptions, cancellation, and concurrent calls
docs.text:
Neither async helper catches thrown exceptions or uses finally to reset loading. If the operation throws, including CancellationException, execution exits without recording a returned failure and can leave loading true. Return a Result for expected operation failures; keep cancellation propagating. The repository's suspendRunCatching boundary is described in Data. Calling getOrThrow() inside a helper is not equivalent to returning the repository Result.

A call that sees loading = true is dropped, rather than queued. The check occurs before launching, but loading is set inside the coroutine. Calls queued before that coroutine runs can both start. This is not a concurrency lock; overlapping completions can clear loading while another operation is still running. The Async state lifecycle follow-up tracks exception cleanup and overlap behavior.

The operation receives a snapshot of data read inside the coroutine. If updateStateWith suspends and later returns a copy of that snapshot, it overwrites synchronous edits made in the meantime. updateWith also receives a snapshot, but does not write it back on completion.

For independent operations, use separate operation state when their loading/error lifetimes need to differ. A single loading flag cannot represent independent progress. As an extension, choose whether to disable edits during save, merge selected result fields into current data, or serialize operations. Those policies require implementation and tests; the helpers do not supply them.

docs.title: Resetting and optimistic updates
docs.text:
An illustrative Item data reset is _itemUiState.updateState { ItemScreenData() }. This resets the form, creates a new ID, and preserves loading/error. Replacing the whole wrapper with _itemUiState.value = UiState(ItemScreenData()) also resets loading/error, but does not cancel an in-flight job; its eventual completion can still write state. Decide how to end or coordinate that job before resetting an active form. Resetting an edited item to a new UUID changes its identity.

The template persists local writes before background synchronization; that does not confirm remote success. An optimistic UI extension that updates display state before local persistence needs explicit failure handling and rollback. Restoring an old snapshot can erase newer edits, so define how concurrent edits are preserved before adding rollback.

docs.title: Context parameters
docs.text:
The async helpers declare context(viewModel: ViewModel) and launch into that ViewModel's viewModelScope. Inside a ViewModel member, Kotlin can supply the enclosing ViewModel context:

// Declaration excerpt; the body is omitted.
context(viewModel: ViewModel) inline fun <reified T : Any> MutableStateFlow<UiState<T>>.updateStateWith(
    crossinline operation: suspend T.() -> Result<T>,
)

The project uses Kotlin 2.4.10 without an explicit -Xcontext-parameters flag. Follow the existing build configuration; no additional flag or dependency is needed to call these helpers.

docs.title: OneTimeEvent<T>
docs.text:
getContentIfNotHandled() atomically marks the wrapper consumed, then returns its content. Later calls return null. A null payload is indistinguishable from an already-consumed event through this method. peekContent() reads without consuming. Competing consumers share one flag; creating a new wrapper creates a new flag, even for equal content.

Consumption does not confirm delivery or completion of navigation/snackbar work, retry cancellation, or persist across process death. The current StatefulComposable consumes during composition and keys its effect on the callback. Existing Compose tests demonstrate two limitations:

  • Recomposition after consumption can remove the effect and cancel an unfinished callback.
  • A new error under the same callback key can be consumed without launching a new callback.

A discarded composition can also consume before committing; this is a source-reviewed risk rather than a reproduced test case. The Event delivery follow-up tracks changing consumption and effect lifetime together.

ItemScreen consumes its navigation event inside an effect instead:

LaunchedEffect(screenData.navigateBack, onBackClick) {
    if (screenData.navigateBack.getContentIfNotHandled() == true) {
        onBackClick()
    }
}

This avoids consuming during the composition body, but still does not acknowledge completed navigation. Do not infer that a plain Boolean necessarily repeats on every recomposition: effect keys and effect lifetime also determine execution. For the current Item save failure behavior, see updateStateWith.

docs.title: Subscription lifetimes
docs.text:
stateInDelayed(initialValue, viewModelScope) shares the upstream with SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5000L). It starts when collected, stops the upstream five seconds after the last subscriber leaves, retains its latest value, and restarts upstream for a later subscriber. Reading .value alone does not start collection.

Home and Item place onStart { getJetpacks() } / onStart { getJetpack() } before this sharing operator. Those methods launch repository collection separately in viewModelScope. When the shared upstream stops, those separate collectors remain active. Restarting it launches another collector; they accumulate until the ViewModel is cleared. Settings uses the same separate-job pattern with a zero sharing timeout. Screen lifecycle collection alone does not fix that lifetime mismatch. The Observation lifetime follow-up includes Profile and preserving locale refresh behavior.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Place the following complete example alongside Item's existing unit tests in feature:home. The module already has the test dependencies. The fake is supplied explicitly; no Hilt test graph or database is needed. Turbine starts collection before editing, so the exposed shared state actually observes the change. This example checks input preservation, not repository persistence.

package dev.atick.feature.home.ui.item

import app.cash.turbine.test
import com.google.common.truth.Truth.assertThat
import dev.atick.core.testing.rule.MainDispatcherRule
import dev.atick.data.model.home.Jetpack
import dev.atick.data.repository.home.HomeRepository
import dev.atick.data.utils.SyncProgress
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.emptyFlow
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest
import org.junit.Rule
import org.junit.Test

class ItemInputExampleTest {
    @get:Rule
    val mainDispatcherRule = MainDispatcherRule()

    @Test
    fun `keeps a trailing decimal point`() = runTest {
        val viewModel = ItemViewModel(InputRepository(), existingJetpackId = null)
        viewModel.itemUiState.test {
            assertThat(awaitItem().data.jetpackPrice).isEmpty()
            viewModel.updatePrice("1.")
            assertThat(awaitItem().data.jetpackPrice).isEqualTo("1.")
            cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()
        }
    }
}

private class InputRepository : HomeRepository {
    override fun getJetpacks(): Flow<List<Jetpack>> = emptyFlow()
    override fun getJetpack(id: String): Flow<Jetpack> = emptyFlow()
    override suspend fun createOrUpdateJetpack(jetpack: Jetpack): Result<Unit> =
        Result.success(Unit)
    override suspend fun markJetpackAsDeleted(jetpack: Jetpack): Result<Unit> =
        Result.success(Unit)
    override suspend fun sync(): Flow<SyncProgress> = emptyFlow()
}

Run ./gradlew :feature:home:testDebugUnitTest. MainDispatcherRule uses an eager test dispatcher by default. That is useful here, but does not exercise calls queued before loading becomes true. Use a controlled dispatcher and suspended operations when testing overlap or edits during save.

The existing suites provide complementary coverage:

Suite Coverage StatefulComposableTest Synchronous transforms, returned success/failure, loading, error reset UiStateContractTest Queued overlap, thrown exceptions, cancellation, suspended edits StatefulComposableEventTest Actual Compose effect cancellation and replacement-error behavior OneTimeEventTest Consumption and peeking, including concurrent access ItemViewModelTest Raw input/parsing, current failed save/load behavior, Home/Item collector accumulation

Tests documenting current defects are characterization tests, not evidence that those behaviors are desirable. Inspect error content with peekContent() when the assertion must not consume it. Clear ViewModel scopes in lifetime tests so their separately launched collectors are cancelled.
